fact: Uses a short, flexible snout to grab leaves, and submerges in rivers to feed and let small fish groom parasites off it.

name: Giant Anteater
fact: Has no teeth at all — a sticky tongue up to 60cm long, flicking around 160 times a minute, does all the work.

name: Opossum
fact: North America's only marsupial — its famous "playing dead" is an involuntary fainting spell, not a decision.

name: Wombat
fact: Digs vast burrow systems and produces cube-shaped droppings — an intestinal trick that stops them rolling away.

name: Mesite
fact: A weak-flying, ground-foraging bird found only in Madagascar's forests.

name: Kagu
fact: A near-flightless bird found only on New Caledonia, hunting earthworms with nostril flaps found on no other bird.

name: Sunbittern
fact: When threatened, it fans its wings to reveal huge fake eyespots, briefly looking like a much larger animal.

name: Turaco
fact: One of the only birds with true green and red feather pigments — most bird "green" is a trick of light, not colour.

name: Hoatzin
fact: Digests leaves by fermenting them in an oversized crop, like a cow — and its chicks are born with claws on their wings.

name: Seriema
fact: The closest living relative of the extinct terror birds, killing prey by beating it against the ground.

name: Cuckoo-roller
fact: The only member of its own bird order — despite the name, unrelated to true cuckoos or true rollers.

name: Tuatara
fact: New Zealand's "living fossil" reptile, the last of its order, with a light-sensing third eye on a hatchling's skull.

name: Amphisbaenian
fact: A limbless burrower whose blunt tail looks so much like its head that some cultures call it "two-headed."

name: Cumulus
fact: A heap cloud built by convection over warm ground, its flat base usually below 550 m.

name: Cirrus
fact: Ice crystals 6,000 to 20,000 m up, combed by strong winds aloft into curls called mare's tails.

name: Stratus
fact: A flat grey sheet under 2,000 m, named for lying in layers. Lower it to the ground and it is fog.

name: Cumulonimbus
fact: A cumulus that kept growing until it hit the tropopause and spread into an anvil, often past 12,000 m.

name: Nimbostratus
fact: A thick dark layer riding in on a warm front, wringing out steady rain or snow for hours.

name: Supercell
fact: A thunderstorm organised around a mesocyclone, a deep updraught that keeps rotating for hours.

name: Monsoon
fact: A seasonal wind that reverses because land heats and cools faster than the ocean beside it.

name: Anticyclone
fact: Sinking air spreads out at the surface as high pressure, clearing the sky it descends through.

name: Low-Pressure System
fact: A mid-latitude cyclone: a warm front and a cold front, rotating together round a shared low.

name: Warm Front
fact: Warm air riding up and over a retreating wedge of cold, denser air — a slow, wide advance.

name: Cold Front
fact: Dense cold air undercutting the warmer air ahead of it, moving up to twice a warm front's speed.

name: Sleet
fact: Snow that melted crossing a warm layer aloft, then refroze into a hard pellet near the ground.

name: Drizzle
fact: Droplets under 0.5 mm across, misted out of a low stratus deck — too light to fall as rain.

name: Anemometer
fact: Four hemispherical cups on a shaft, spun by wind pressure. Robinson's design, 1846.

discovered.note: John Thomas Romney Robinson builds the four-cup anemometer.

name: Rain Gauge
fact: A funnel over a graduated cylinder. Korea's cheugugi, standardised in 1441, was the first of its kind.

discovered.note: The cheugugi rain gauge is standardised across Joseon Korea under King Sejong.

name: Weather Vane
fact: An asymmetric pointer that swings to face into the wind. Athens' Tower of the Winds carried a bronze one.

name: Hygrometer
fact: Human hair lengthens as humidity rises. De Saussure built the first hair hygrometer from one in 1783.

discovered.note: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure builds a hygrometer using a strand of human hair.

name: Tropical Climate
fact: Köppen's line for it: every month averages 18°C or warmer. There is no real winter here.

name: Arid Climate
fact: Defined by evaporation outrunning rainfall, not by temperature — deserts and dry steppe both qualify.

name: Temperate Climate
fact: The mid-latitude belt, 23.5° to 66.5°, where most of humanity lives through four real seasons.

name: Mercury
fact: 70% metal by mass, giving it the largest iron core of any planet by volume — 57% of it.

name: Venus
fact: 96.5% carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat so well it beats Mercury for hottest planet.

name: Earth
fact: The only known world with stable liquid water on its surface, covering 71% of it.

name: Mars
fact: Iron oxide dust rusted red over billions of years — hence the nickname, the Red Planet.

name: Jupiter
fact: Radiates more heat than it gets from the Sun, still shrinking from its own formation.

name: Saturn
fact: The only planet less dense than water — a big enough bathtub and it would float.

name: Uranus
fact: Coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system, -224°C, though not the farthest out.

name: Neptune
fact: Found by math before anyone saw it — Le Verrier calculated it, Galle spotted it in 1846.

name: Pluto
fact: Largest known body in the Kuiper belt by volume, found by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930.

name: Io
fact: The most volcanically active body in the solar system, squeezed by Jupiter's tides.

name: Europa
fact: An icy shell over an ocean holding two to three times the water of every ocean on Earth.

name: Ganymede
fact: Bigger than Mercury and the only moon known to make its own magnetic field.

name: Callisto
fact: The most heavily cratered surface known — unchanged and un-resurfaced for 4.5 billion years.

name: Saturn's Rings
fact: 99.9% pure water ice, in pieces from dust grains to houses, spread out paper-thin.

name: Cassini Division
fact: A 4,800 km gap Cassini spotted in 1675, swept clear by the moon Mimas's gravity.

name: Titan
fact: The only moon with a thick atmosphere, and lakes of liquid methane on its surface.

name: Enceladus
fact: Geysers of ice erupt from its south pole, feeding Saturn's E ring, seen by Cassini in 2005.

name: Mimas
fact: One crater a third of its own width away from looking exactly like the Death Star.

name: Titania
fact: Uranus's largest moon, half ice half rock, scarred by a 1,500 km canyon.

name: Oberon
fact: Its reddish, crater-pocked face hides an unexplained 11 km peak near the south pole.

name: Miranda
fact: Jumbled chevron terrain and a 20 km cliff suggest it was shattered and re-assembled.

name: Triton
fact: Orbits Neptune backward — the sign of a captured world, not one born in place.

name: Phobos
fact: Spiraling inward toward Mars; in 30-50 million years it will crash or shred into a ring.

name: Deimos
fact: Found six days before its sibling Phobos, and drifting away from Mars, not toward it.

name: Charon
fact: Pluto and Charon orbit a point outside Pluto itself, each always showing the other one face.

name: Ceres
fact: Holds 40% of the asteroid belt's mass, a quarter of it water ice, found in 1801.

name: Eris
fact: 27% more massive than Pluto — the discovery in 2005 that got Pluto demoted.

name: Great Red Spot
fact: A storm wider than Earth, tracked continuously since 1878 and still shrinking.

name: Longship
fact: Clinker-built Viking warship with one square sail of rough wool -- shallow enough to row up rivers.

name: Viking
fact: Norse seafarers and raiders; their word vikingr is rare before the 1100s, mostly seen on runestones.

name: L'Anse aux Meadows
fact: Norse base camp in Newfoundland, tree-ring dated to 1021 CE -- Europe's earliest footprint in the Americas.

name: Castle
fact: Malbork Castle in Poland, finished 1406, is the world's largest brick castle -- walls enclosing 21 hectares.

name: Moat
fact: A defensive ditch around a fortification, dry or water-filled, keeping siege engines off the walls.

name: Drawbridge
fact: A castle's moat-crossing bridge, pivoted at the gatehouse and winched up by chain to seal the entrance shut.

name: Colosseum
fact: Rome's amphitheatre, finished 80 CE, seated up to 80,000 for gladiator bouts and staged animal hunts.

name: Gladiator
fact: Rome's arena fighters; the earliest were prisoners of war, named and armed after the enemies Rome just beat.

name: Great Wall of China
fact: Ming builders bonded its bricks with mortar of slaked lime and sticky-rice soup -- stronger than lime alone.

name: Caravel
fact: Portuguese ship with a narrow hull and lateen sails, able to sail closer to the wind than a square-rigger.

name: Christopher Columbus
fact: Crossed the Atlantic in 1492 on a fleet including two caravels, and insisted for years he had reached Asia.

name: Hardtack
fact: Flour, water, and salt baked into a dense unleavened cracker, dry enough to survive months at sea unspoiled.

name: Hoba Meteorite
fact: The largest intact meteorite ever found -- a 60-tonne iron-nickel mass a plough struck in Namibia in 1920.

name: Tickle
fact: The cerebellum predicts the feel of your own touch and dampens it, which is why you can't tickle yourself.

name: Sneeze
fact: A nerve reflex fired by nasal irritants; high-speed video has caught its plume carrying 8 meters.

name: Bitumen
fact: Petroleum's heaviest fraction — what's left once everything lighter than 500°C boils away.

name: Archimedes' Screw
fact: A helical blade in a tube lifts water as it turns. Traditionally credited to Archimedes, 3rd century BC.

discovered.note: Traditionally credited to Archimedes, though it may predate him.

name: Elephant Clock
fact: A sinking float trips a see-saw every half hour, dropping a ball to strike a bell. al-Jazari, 1206.

discovered.note: al-Jazari describes it in The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices.

name: Crankshaft
fact: Turns circular motion into back-and-forth motion, or the reverse. al-Jazari's water-raising pump, 1206.

discovered.note: al-Jazari combines a crank with a connecting rod in a twin-cylinder water pump.

name: Submarine
fact: A leather-covered wooden hull, rowed underwater by oars sealed through the sides. Drebbel, 1620.

discovered.note: Drebbel demonstrates the first navigable submarine beneath the Thames.

name: Thermostat
fact: Expanding mercury pushes a lever that closes a damper — an early feedback-controlled device. Drebbel, 1620s.

discovered.note: Drebbel builds a self-regulating mercury thermostat for a chicken incubator.

name: Lightning Rod
fact: A grounded iron point gives a stroke somewhere safe to go instead of the building beneath it. Franklin, 1752.

discovered.note: Franklin proposes the pointed, grounded lightning rod.

name: Bifocals
fact: Two lenses' halves set in one frame, near vision below and far above. Franklin is generally credited, by 1784.

discovered.note: Franklin is generally credited with combining two half-lenses in one frame.

name: Centrifugal Governor
fact: Spinning flyweights swing outward as speed rises and choke the throttle. Watt, 1788.

discovered.note: Watt adapts the flyball governor, already used on windmills, to regulate his steam engine.

name: Heliography
fact: Bitumen hardens where light strikes it; washing off the rest leaves the world's first photo. Niépce, c.1827.

discovered.note: Niépce fixes a permanent image on a bitumen-coated pewter plate.

name: Antiseptic Dressing
fact: Cotton soaked in undiluted carbolic acid, packed onto a wound. Lister's first case, 1865.

discovered.note: Lister soaks cotton dressings in carbolic acid to treat a compound fracture.

name: Blasting Cap
fact: A small charge that detonates a bigger one it can't ignite by itself. Nobel adds mercury fulminate, 1867.

discovered.note: Nobel packs mercury fulminate into a copper capsule to reliably detonate nitroglycerin.

name: Automobile
fact: A single-cylinder engine bolted to a three-wheeled carriage — the first car built for sale. Benz, 1885–86.

discovered.note: Benz patents the Motorwagen, the first automobile put into production.

name: Metal Detector
fact: Two induction coils balance against each other until metal nearby throws them off. Bell, 1881.

discovered.note: Bell builds an induction-balance detector searching for the bullet in President Garfield.

name: Tesla Coil
fact: Two coils tuned to the same resonant frequency step a spark-gap pulse up to very high voltage. Tesla, 1891.

discovered.note: Tesla patents his resonant air-core transformer circuit.

name: AC Induction Motor
fact: A rotating magnetic field drags an unpowered rotor around with it — no brushes needed. Tesla, 1887–88.

discovered.note: Tesla patents his alternating-current induction motor.

name: Autogyro
fact: A propeller pulls it forward while an unpowered rotor autorotates and lifts it. de la Cierva, 1923.

discovered.note: de la Cierva flies the first autogyro, lifted by an unpowered, freely autorotating rotor.

name: Liquid-Fuel Rocket
fact: Ethanol and liquid oxygen burn through an alloy nozzle built to survive it. Von Braun's V-2, 1942.

discovered.note: Von Braun's V-2, burning ethanol and liquid oxygen, becomes the first rocket to reach space.

name: Enigma Machine
fact: A keyboard and wired rotors light one of 26 lamps per keystroke, a different letter. Scherbius, 1918.

discovered.note: Scherbius patents the rotor cipher machine.

name: Bombe
fact: Electromechanical drums replicate dozens of Enigma rotor settings at once, ruling most out. Turing, 1939.

discovered.note: Turing designs the British bombe at Bletchley Park to find the Enigma's daily settings.

name: Mercaptopurine
fact: A purine ring with sulfur where guanine has oxygen — it jams DNA synthesis in dividing cells. Elion, 1953.

discovered.note: Elion and Hitchings develop it at Burroughs Wellcome as the first chemotherapy for childhood leukemia.

name: Hypertext
fact: Text wired with links a reader can jump through, instead of reading straight down the page. Nelson, 1965.

name: World Wide Web
fact: Berners-Lee married hypertext to the Internet: one naming scheme, one protocol, one markup language. 1989–91.

discovered.note: Berners-Lee builds HTTP, HTML, the URL and the first browser and server at CERN.

name: Ichthyosaur
fact: Joseph Anning found the skull in 1811; his sister Mary spent months excavating the rest of the skeleton.

discovered.note: Mary Anning completes excavating the first Ichthyosaurus skeleton to draw scientific attention, at Lyme Regis.

name: Leprosy
fact: Mycobacterium leprae divides so slowly that symptoms can take five years or more to appear.

name: Chaulmoogra Ester
fact: Alice Ball turned chaulmoogra oil's fatty acids into ethyl esters in 1916 — finally soluble enough to inject.

discovered.note: Alice Ball develops the ethyl-ester method at the University of Hawaii, but dies before publishing it herself.

name: Artemisinin
fact: Sweet wormwood's antimalarial compound — heat destroys it, so the extraction has to stay cold.

discovered.note: Tu Youyou's team isolates artemisinin; she shares the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

name: Lamarckism
fact: Lamarck's giraffe: a neck stretched in one lifetime, passed on already lengthened to the next.

discovered.note: Lamarck publishes Philosophie Zoologique, proposing that acquired traits pass to offspring.

name: ABO Blood Group
fact: Mix the wrong two and red cells clump together — why blood gets typed before a transfusion.

discovered.note: Karl Landsteiner publishes the ABO system; he receives the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.

name: Waggle Dance
fact: A bee's waggle run points at an angle from vertical equal to the food's angle from the Sun.

name: Book of Optics
fact: Argued vision happens because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays.

discovered.note: Ibn al-Haytham completes the seven-volume Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir).

name: Event Horizon Telescope
fact: Linked telescopes worldwide into one Earth-sized dish and imaged a black hole's shadow, 2019.

discovered.note: The EHT Collaboration releases the first image of a black hole, M87*, on 10 April 2019.

name: Sapling
fact: A young tree past the seedling stage: its stem has turned from soft and green to properly woody.

name: Cambium
fact: A ring of dividing cells under the bark — it builds new xylem inward and new phloem outward each year.

name: Sapwood
fact: The living outer wood of a trunk, still carrying water up from the roots before it hardens into heartwood.

name: Heartwood
fact: The dead, dark core of an old trunk — chemically toughened sapwood that still braces the tree once it's gone.

name: Cone
fact: A conifer's seed case — it ripens over months, and some species keep it sealed shut on the tree for years.

name: Conifer
fact: Cone-bearing, needle- or scale-leaved, and mostly evergreen — pines, firs, cedars and cypresses among them.

name: Gymnosperm
fact: A seed plant with naked seeds — no fruit wrapped around them, unlike an angiosperm's.

name: Abscission
fact: The layer of cork cells a plant grows across a leaf stalk, which is what actually makes the leaf fall.

name: Deciduous
fact: Sheds its leaves on a seasonal cue rather than keeping them through winter like an evergreen does.

name: Samara
fact: A winged seed shaped like a tiny airfoil — maple and ash both spin theirs down like a helicopter blade.

name: Catkin
fact: A dangling, petal-less flower spike built for wind pollination, not for attracting insects.

name: Larch
fact: A conifer that breaks its own family's rule: it drops its needles every autumn like a broadleaf tree.

name: Cedar
fact: A resinous evergreen conifer with barrel-shaped cones that disintegrate scale by scale on the tree.

name: Juniper
fact: A conifer whose cone scales fuse into a fleshy, berry-like ball — the 'berries' that flavour gin.

name: Holly
fact: Spiny, glossy evergreen leaves and red winter berries — festive to look at, mildly toxic if eaten.

name: Magnolia
fact: An ancient flowering tree — its lineage predates bees, so beetles still do the pollinating.

name: Maple
fact: Winged samara seeds, and in some species sap sweet enough to boil down into syrup.

name: Birch
fact: Thin, papery bark that peels off in horizontal strips, and catkins instead of showy flowers.

name: Beech
fact: Smooth grey bark and 'mast' — oil-rich beechnuts once used to fatten pigs before winter.

name: Elm
fact: Its bark carries the beetle that spreads the fungus behind Dutch elm disease.

name: Eucalyptus
fact: Oil-rich leaves toxic to most browsers — koalas are among the few animals that can stomach them.

name: Baobab
fact: A trunk swollen enough to store up to 120,000 litres of water against the next drought.

name: Banyan
fact: Sends roots straight down from its branches; each one thickens into another trunk until it's a forest.

name: Aspen
fact: Its leaf stalks are flattened sideways, so even a light breeze sets the whole canopy quaking.

name: Rootstock
fact: The rooted half of a graft — swap it and you can dwarf a full-size apple tree without touching the fruit.

name: Scion
fact: The cutting grafted onto a rootstock — every graft of it is a genetic clone of one original tree.

name: Crabapple
fact: Grow an apple from its own seed and you get this: small, sour, and nothing like its parent.

name: Chill Hours
fact: The quota of winter cold a fruit tree must clock up before it will flower properly in spring.

name: Breadfruit
fact: Starchy enough to be a staple food across the Pacific — baked, boiled or fried, never eaten raw.

name: Jackfruit
fact: The largest fruit grown on any tree, up to 55 kg, in the same genus as breadfruit.

name: Lychee
fact: A rind hiding a translucent, sweet aril wrapped around one seed — botanically, a drupe.

name: Rambutan
fact: Lychee's spiky cousin in the soapberry family — its name is just Malay for 'hair.'

name: Longan
fact: Lychee's other cousin, named for the way its black seed shows through the flesh like an eye.

name: Tamarind
fact: A legume tree — its pod fruit is sour enough to season food across three continents.

name: Dragon Fruit
fact: The fruit of a climbing cactus, one that scales trees for support without ever rooting in them.

name: Starfruit
fact: Slice it crosswise and its five ridges turn every piece into a perfect star.

name: Soursop
fact: A relative of the custard apple and cherimoya, with spiny green skin and soft, custardy pulp.

name: Akee
fact: Jamaica's national fruit — and toxic until its own capsule splits open on the tree.

name: Curry Leaf
fact: Fried in hot oil at the start of a dish, which is how its aroma actually gets released.

name: Control Rod
fact: Slides into the reactor core to soak up neutrons and choke off the chain reaction on demand.

name: Nuclear Reactor
fact: The same fission as a bomb, just held on the edge of runaway instead of let loose.

name: Corium
fact: Chernobyl's 'elephant's foot' — fuel, control rods and structure melted into one radioactive lava.

name: Nuclear Power Plant
fact: The reactor never spins anything itself — it just boils water for a turbine to do that.

name: Heat Shield Tile
fact: Silica fiber fired so light it's 90% empty space, yet it shrugged off 1,260°C on re-entry.

name: Tunnel Boring Machine
fact: A rotating steel cutterhead chews the tunnel face while hydraulic rams shove the machine forward.

name: CT Scanner
fact: An X-ray tube and detectors spin around the patient; a computer stacks the angles into 3D.

name: Hydroelectric Dam
fact: Water drops through a penstock into a turbine — a whole river's fall, spent turning one shaft.

name: Stand Mixer
fact: Named for its beater's own motion — it spins on its own axis while orbiting the bowl, like a planet.

name: Swashplate
fact: A tilting plate that changes each rotor blade's pitch differently through the turn — how a helicopter steers.

name: Electric Car
fact: No engine, no gearbox, no idle — a battery and a motor with full torque from a dead stop.

name: Icebreaker
fact: Doesn't climb the ice and crush it — a reinforced bow bends and breaks it under the hull at speed.

name: Snow Groomer
fact: A tracked tiller combs the piste into corduroy, winched up the steepest slopes on a cable.

name: Turboprop
fact: A gas turbine that barely bothers with jet thrust — a gearbox sends nearly all its power to a propeller.

name: M1 Abrams
fact: A tank engine borrowed from an idea more common in helicopters — a 1,500hp gas turbine, not a diesel.

name: Tiger Tank
fact: Flat, vertical armor plates and an 88mm gun — no sloping, unlike its own stablemate the Panther.

name: Radar
fact: Times a radio echo's round trip — half the delay, times the speed of light, is the range.

name: Stealth Aircraft
fact: Faceted panels fling radar's echo away from the receiver instead of straight back at it.

name: Rivet
fact: Driven red-hot through two plates and hammered into a second head, it only clamps tight once it cools.

name: Ocean Liner
fact: Watertight bulkheads split the hull into compartments — Titanic's simply didn't reach high enough.

name: Elliptical Wing
fact: The lift distribution with the least induced drag of any wing planform — the Spitfire's signature shape.

name: Box
fact: A rigid container, traditionally built from flat wooden panels joined edge to edge and nailed.

name: Veil
fact: A piece of fine, often sheer cloth worn to cover the head or face, traditionally woven in silk.

name: Socrates
fact: Athenian philosopher executed in 399 BCE for impiety and corrupting the youth; wrote nothing himself.

name: Plato
fact: Student of Socrates; founded The Academy in Athens in 387 BCE, Europe's first university.

name: Aristotle
fact: Tutored the young Alexander the Great and founded The Lyceum, teaching logic, biology, and physics.

name: René Descartes
fact: French philosopher and mathematician who united algebra and geometry into the coordinate system.

name: John Locke
fact: English philosopher who argued the mind at birth is a blank slate, filled only by experience.

name: Immanuel Kant
fact: German philosopher who argued morality rests on unbreakable, universal rules reason gives itself.

name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
fact: Austrian philosopher of language and logic who gave away his fortune to teach village schoolchildren.

name: Simone de Beauvoir
fact: French existentialist philosopher and author of The Second Sex, a founding text of modern feminism.

name: Confucius
fact: Chinese philosopher and teacher whose sayings on virtue and reciprocity fill the Analects.

name: Buddha
fact: Born Siddhartha Gautama, a prince who renounced his palace and, on reaching enlightenment, became the Buddha.

name: Avicenna
fact: Persian polymath and physician whose Canon of Medicine was a standard European textbook for 600 years.

name: Plutarch
fact: Greek-born biographer and priest at the Delphic oracle who wrote the paired Lives of Greeks and Romans.

name: Epicurus
fact: Athenian philosopher who taught in a garden school, The Garden, that unusually admitted women as students.

name: John Searle
fact: American philosopher who devised the Chinese Room argument against machine understanding in 1980.

name: Alan Turing
fact: British mathematician who laid computing's theoretical foundation and devised a test for machine intelligence.

name: Philippa Foot
fact: British philosopher who devised the runaway-tram dilemma known as the trolley problem in 1967.

name: John Rawls
fact: American philosopher who devised the 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment for choosing a just society.

name: Thomas Aquinas
fact: Dominican friar and theologian who argued from motion to an unmoved first mover he called God.

name: Martin Heidegger
fact: German philosopher whose Being and Time argued the meaning of Being is inseparable from time and mortality.

name: Jean-Paul Sartre
fact: French existentialist who argued human existence precedes essence — we exist first, then define ourselves.

name: Albert Camus
fact: French-Algerian philosopher who argued we must imagine Sisyphus happy, embracing the absurdity of existence.

name: Hannah Arendt
fact: German-American theorist who covered Eichmann's 1961 trial and coined 'the banality of evil.'

name: Michel Foucault
fact: French philosopher who used the all-seeing prison tower called the Panopticon as a metaphor for modern power.

name: Jacques Derrida
fact: French philosopher who coined 'différance,' a difference invisible in speech and legible only in writing.

name: Karl Popper
fact: Austrian-British philosopher who argued a theory counts as scientific only if a single test could disprove it.

name: Thomas Kuhn
fact: American philosopher of science who argued science advances through revolutionary paradigm shifts.

name: Noam Chomsky
fact: American linguist and critic who argued mass media manufactures public consent for state and corporate power.

name: Peter Singer
fact: Australian philosopher whose 1975 book Animal Liberation founded the modern animal rights movement.

name: William of Ockham
fact: English Franciscan friar remembered for the principle that the simplest sufficient explanation is best.

name: Ayn Rand
fact: Russian-American novelist who founded Objectivism, prizing rational self-interest over altruism.

name: Edward Said
fact: Palestinian-American scholar whose Orientalism argued Western depictions of 'the East' served empire.

name: Jurgen Habermas
fact: German philosopher who traced the modern public sphere of reasoned debate to 18th-century coffeehouses.

name: Isaiah Berlin
fact: Latvian-British philosopher who distinguished freedom from restraint from freedom to control one's own fate.

name: Theodor Adorno
fact: German philosopher who coined 'culture industry' for mass media manufacturing passive, uncritical consumers.

name: Herbert Marcuse
fact: German-American philosopher who argued consumer society manufactures false needs to suppress dissent.

name: Emmanuel Levinas
fact: Lithuanian-French philosopher who argued ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter, before any reasoning.

name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
fact: French phenomenologist who rejected Descartes' mind-body split, arguing consciousness is always embodied.

name: Willard Van Orman Quine
fact: American logician who argued translating between languages is fundamentally indeterminate.

name: Roland Barthes
fact: French theorist whose essay 'The Death of the Author' argued a text's meaning outlives its writer's intent.

name: Frantz Fanon
fact: Martinican psychiatrist whose Black Skin, White Masks examined colonialism's psychological toll.

name: Arne Naess
fact: Norwegian philosopher who coined 'deep ecology,' urging humans to see themselves as part of nature.

name: Giordano Bruno
fact: Italian friar burned at the stake in 1600 for insisting the universe is infinite, filled with countless suns.

name: Gilbert Ryle
fact: British philosopher who mocked Cartesian dualism as belief in 'the ghost in the machine.'

name: J. L. Austin
fact: British philosopher who showed some sentences perform an action rather than describe the world.

name: René Girard
fact: French thinker who traced religion and violence to a 'scapegoat mechanism' uniting a group against one victim.

name: Daniel Dennett
fact: American philosopher who argued there is no single place in the brain where consciousness happens.

name: Martha Nussbaum
fact: American philosopher who, with Amartya Sen, developed the 'capabilities approach' to justice and flourishing.

name: Hypatia of Alexandria
fact: Alexandrian mathematician and astronomer who taught astrolabe-making and was murdered by a mob in 415 CE.

name: Sodium Hydroxide
fact: Caustic soda. Dissolving it in water alone gives off enough heat to bring the water to a boil.

name: Potassium Hydroxide
fact: Caustic potash. Its soaps stay soft where sodium hydroxide's go hard.

name: Calcium Hydroxide
fact: Slaked lime, dissolved as limewater — a jar left open clouds within minutes, coated by the CO2 it tests for.

name: Ethane
fact: The second-biggest thing in natural gas after methane, mostly there to be cracked back into ethylene.

name: Hydrogen Peroxide
fact: Kept in dark bottles for a reason: light alone is enough to break it back down into water and oxygen.

name: Silver Nitrate
fact: Darkens skin black over hours as organic matter reduces the silver — the same stain old election inks left on voters.

name: Potassium Acetate
fact: E261. Airports spray it on runways instead of chloride salts — just as effective, far gentler on the concrete.

name: Zinc Chloride
fact: So hygroscopic a jar left open pulls enough water from the air to dissolve itself into a puddle by morning.

name: Hydrochloric acid
fact: Hydrogen chloride dissolved in water — commercial grades run up to 38%, about as strong as it ships.

name: Sodium carbonate
fact: Washing soda, Na2CO3 — the alkali glassmakers have used to lower sand's melting point for millennia.

name: Aluminium sulfate
fact: Al2(SO4)3 — dumped into cloudy water by the tonne, it drags suspended grit down into a settleable clump.

name: Ammonium phosphate
fact: (NH4)3PO4 and its relatives — most of the world's phosphate fertiliser starts as this salt.

name: Carbon tetrachloride
fact: CCl4 — a non-flammable solvent banned once its liver toxicity and ozone damage were understood.

name: Magnesium phosphate
fact: Mg3(PO4)2 and its relatives — magnesium's salts with phosphate, all on the FDA's food-safe list.

name: Sodium sulfate
fact: Na2SO4 — first isolated in 1625 by Glauber, who named it sal mirabilis, the miraculous salt.

name: Ammonium bicarbonate
fact: NH4HCO3 — old-world 'hartshorn', a leavener that gasses off completely and leaves no aftertaste.

name: Ammonium chloride
fact: NH4Cl, sal ammoniac — ninety percent of it becomes nitrogen fertiliser for rice and wheat.

name: Calcium nitrate
fact: Ca(NO3)2 — pulls water from the air so eagerly it needs sealed storage; first made in Norway, 1905.

name: Barium nitrate
fact: Ba(NO3)2 — an oxidiser that burns with a hard green flame, and toxic if swallowed.

name: Calcium acetate
fact: Ca(CH3COO)2, E263 — vinegar poured straight onto limestone or eggshell, made this way for millennia.

name: Phosphoric acid
fact: H3PO4 — the tang in cola. Ninety percent of the world's output becomes fertiliser instead.

name: Sodium phosphate
fact: Na3PO4 — strongly alkaline in water, used as everything from a food buffer to a heavy-duty degreaser.

name: Chromium Oxide
fact: Chrome green, and the reason chromium itself does not rust — a film one molecule thick that heals itself.

name: Manganese Dioxide
fact: Half a million tonnes a year go into one job: soaking up electrons inside an ordinary dry-cell battery.

name: Rhubarb
fact: The edible part is only the leaf stalk. The leaf blade itself is poisonous — oxalic acid.

name: Hydrogen Bromide
fact: Hydrogen and bromine, combined between 200 and 400°C, usually over a platinum catalyst.

name: Sodium citrate
fact: Citric acid neutralised into a calm, food-safe salt — E331, and the anticoagulant in a bag of donated blood.

name: Sodium nitrite
fact: NaNO2, E250 — the curing salt that turns cured meat pink and holds back botulinum spores.

name: Sulfate
fact: SO4²⁻ — one sulfur, four oxygens, the ion sulfuric acid leaves behind and acid rain deposits.

name: Barium sulfide
fact: BaS — calcined straight from the elements, and it glows in the dark after exposure to light.

name: Barium carbonate
fact: Witherite. Soluble enough in stomach acid that it used to be sold as rat poison.

name: Hydrogen sulfate
fact: HSO4⁻ — sulfuric acid's first proton gone, and sulfate's second still to lose.

name: Permanganate
fact: MnO4⁻, deep purple in solution — the ion a titration is judged by, because its own colour is the endpoint.

name: Silver phosphate
fact: Ag3PO4 — a yellow precipitate, light-sensitive like silver's other insoluble salts.

name: Silver oxide
fact: Ag2O — dark brown, and what a silver-oxide button battery actually runs on at the cathode.

name: Ammonium bromide
fact: NH4Br — a straightforward gas-phase handshake between ammonia and hydrogen bromide.

name: Calcium phosphate
fact: Ca3(PO4)2 — the anticaking agent in powdered spices, and the mineral half of bone once a hydroxide joins it.

name: Sodium chromate
fact: Na2CrO4, bright yellow — chromium(III) oxidised and pulled into alkaline solution.

name: Dichromate
fact: Cr2O7²⁻, orange — the same chromium as yellow chromate, just caught on the acid side of a pH swing.

name: Fructose
fact: Fruit sugar — the sweetest common sugar, and glucose's isomer, atom for atom.

name: Potassium cyanide
fact: KCN — colourless, sugar-like, and the reagent gold mining runs on to pull metal out of crushed ore.

name: Zinc phosphate
fact: Zn3(PO4)2 — the conversion coating etched onto bare steel before primer goes on.

name: Para-dichlorobenzene
fact: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene — the mothball smell, and benzene with two hydrogens swapped for chlorine.

name: Oxalate
fact: C2O4²⁻ — the ion rhubarb leaves and spinach both carry enough of to matter.

name: Potassium bicarbonate
fact: KHCO3 — potassium's answer to baking soda, and the base of Purple-K fire-extinguisher powder.

name: Potassium hypochlorite
fact: KOCl — the original Eau de Javel, before sodium hypochlorite replaced it as the cheaper bleach.

name: Potassium nitrite
fact: KNO2, E249 — potassium's own curing salt, distinct from potassium nitrate despite the name.

name: Moraine
fact: A glacier works like a conveyor belt: it carries stone for miles and drops it all at the melting end.

name: Breccia
fact: Sharp-edged rock rubble, cemented in place. Nothing wore the corners round, because it never travelled.

name: Arkose
fact: Feldspar-rich sandstone. Feldspar this fresh only survives burial that outraces the rain that would rot it.

name: Graywacke
fact: Sand, mud and rock scraps dumped together by one turbid underwater current, with no time left to sort them.

name: Tillite
fact: Till, buried and hardened. Poorly sorted, striated stones with no layering — a glacier's leftovers, in rock.

name: Chert
fact: Microcrystalline quartz. Ocean-floor ooze of diatom and radiolarian skeletons, slowly turned to solid stone.

name: Ooid
fact: A grain rolled again and again through shallow, chalky water until it grew its own concentric rind.

name: Banded Iron Formation
fact: Iron oxide and chert, laminated in bands — a record of the exact stretch of time oxygen first filled the sea.

name: Anhydrite
fact: Gypsum with the water baked out. It grabs the water straight back the moment it touches any.

name: Oil Shale
fact: Shale packed with kerogen that never got hot enough to finish cooking into petroleum.

name: Phosphorite
fact: Fish bone and scale, concentrated by upwelling into phosphate-rich rock — fertiliser's raw material.

name: Stoneware
fact: Fired hard enough to hold liquid without a glaze.

name: Necktie
fact: Croatian mercenaries wore knotted neckerchiefs in 1630s France; the French called them cravates.

name: Toes
fact: Fourteen small bones in one foot are just for the toes — two in the big toe, three in each other.

name: Toilet Paper
fact: Perforated so a sheet tears free without scissors — patented in Albany, New York, in 1883.

name: Toilet
fact: An S-shaped pipe traps a plug of standing water that seals the drain against sewer gas. Cumming, 1775.

name: Saliva
fact: About 99% water; the rest is mucus and the amylase that starts breaking down starch in the mouth.

name: Tongue
fact: A muscular hydrostat, like an elephant's trunk — no bones, shaped entirely by its own muscle.

name: Bristle
fact: Coarse hair cut from a boar's back and neck, stiff enough to hold its shape packed in a tuft.

name: Toothbrush
fact: William Addis carved the first mass-produced one from a bone handle and boar bristles in 1780.

name: Toy
fact: Egyptian 'paddle dolls' buried with the dead had hair of black Nile-mud beads threaded on string.

name: Towel
fact: The loop pile that soaks up water is called terry — from Turkish hammam cloth, 17th-century Bursa.

name: Tractor
fact: Bolting an engine onto a plough's running gear let one machine pull what used to take a team of horses.

name: Train
fact: A locomotive coupled to any number of unpowered wagons — the wagons don't move themselves.

name: Triangle
fact: A steel rod bent into a triangle with one corner left open, so it rings without a fixed pitch.

name: Tricycle
fact: A third wheel trades a bicycle's need for balance for standing stability. Farffler's hand-cranked chair, 1680.

name: Stomach
fact: Its own lining constantly makes the mucus that keeps stomach acid from digesting the stomach itself.

name: Umbrella
fact: Folding steel ribs replaced heavy, hard-to-fold wood or whalebone frames. Samuel Fox, 1852.

name: Underwear
fact: Linen underclothes go back as far as flax has been woven — worn next to skin for millennia.

name: Vacuum Cleaner
fact: James Spangler's 1907 motor spun a fan and packed dust into a pillowcase sewn onto the machine.

name: Toy Wagon
fact: Antonio Pasin, an Italian immigrant, hand-built his first pull-wagon in a one-room New York shop, 1917.

name: Washcloth
fact: A terrycloth square about 12 by 12 inches — a towel scaled down to fit one hand.

name: Watch
fact: A coiled mainspring replaced hanging weights, letting a clock's movement finally shrink to pocket size.

name: Whistle
fact: A trapped pea rattling inside the chamber breaks the airstream into a trill a smooth tube can't make.

name: Window
fact: Small triangular nails called glazier's points pin the pane into its frame before the putty seals it.

name: Yo-yo
fact: A string looped, not tied, around the axle is what lets it 'sleep' and spin. Flores, 1928.

name: Zipper
fact: Gideon Sundback's interlocking brass teeth, patented 1917, finally made the fastener reliable.

name: Iron(II) Sulfate
fact: FeSO4, pale green crystals also called copperas or green vitriol — dissolve iron in acid instead of burning it in chlorine, and you get the +2 salt instead of the +3 one.

name: Hydrogen Cyanide
fact: HCN — a gas with a faint bitter-almond smell, except that about half of people carry a genetic trait that means they can't smell it at all.

name: Methyl Formate
fact: The simplest ester there is, HCOOCH3 — light enough to boil at just 32°C, and industry's usual route in to formic acid.

name: Sodium Chlorate
fact: NaClO3, chlorine pushed into two different oxidation states in the same reaction. It's potent enough as a total weedkiller that several countries now restrict who can buy it.

name: Chlorine Dioxide
fact: ClO2, an unstable yellow-green gas that can't be shipped or stored — anyone who uses it industrially has to make it fresh, on site, as needed.

name: Sodium Perchlorate
fact: NaClO4, chlorine pushed all the way to its highest possible oxidation state, +7. Its ammonium cousin is the oxidiser packed into solid rocket boosters.

name: Barium Chlorate
fact: Ba(ClO3)2 burns with a deep green firework flame — the same barium that shows up on an X-ray also colours the light when it burns.

name: Barium Chlorite
fact: Ba(ClO2)2 — chlorine's rarest common oxidation state, +3, and really only useful as the one practical door into chlorous acid.

name: Nitrous Acid
fact: HNO2 — too unstable to bottle. It only exists in cold, dilute solution before it falls apart into nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide and water.

name: Hypochlorous Acid
fact: HOCl — the molecule actually doing the disinfecting in chlorinated water and in bleach. Your own white blood cells make it too, to kill bacteria.

name: Chlorous Acid
fact: HClO2, the least stable of chlorine's four common oxoacids and the only one with no industrial use of its own — its salts, the chlorites, are what people actually want.

name: Chloric Acid
fact: HClO3 stays stable only in solution below about 30% strength; push it more concentrated than that and it starts decomposing on its own.

name: Perchloric Acid
fact: HClO4 — one of the strongest acids there is, and hot concentrated solutions of it are such a powerful oxidiser that labs handle it only inside a dedicated, water-washed fume hood.

name: Phosphorous Acid
fact: H3PO3 — despite the name, only two of its three hydrogens are acidic. The third is bonded straight to the phosphorus atom and never lets go.

name: Oxalic Acid
fact: Two carboxyl groups bonded straight to each other with no carbon chain between — the simplest dicarboxylic acid there is, and the same compound that makes rhubarb leaves dangerous.

name: Boric Acid
fact: B(OH)3 — mild enough to have been used as an eyewash, yet sold in the same aisle as roach powder. The dose and the target make all the difference.

name: Silicic Acid
fact: What quartz slowly becomes in water: SiO2 + H2O ⇌ H2SiO3, a reaction Berzelius worked out in the early 1800s and still how silicon ends up dissolved in every river and ocean.

name: Ammonium Hydroxide
fact: What household ammonia actually is — ammonia gas dissolved in water, not a hydroxide compound anyone has ever isolated pure.

name: Magnesium Hydroxide
fact: Mg(OH)2 suspended in water is milk of magnesia; the mineral form of the same exact compound is called brucite.

name: Barium Hydroxide
fact: Ba(OH)2 — one of the few strong bases that isn't an alkali metal hydroxide, made simply by dropping barium oxide into water.

name: Aluminum Hydroxide
fact: Al(OH)3 is amphoteric — it can react as either an acid or a base — and water-treatment plants exploit exactly that to drag suspended dirt out of drinking water.

name: Ferrous Hydroxide (Iron II Hydroxide)
fact: Fe(OH)2 is a pale green solid that doesn't stay pale green for long — open air oxidises it to the reddish-brown +3 hydroxide within minutes.

name: Ferric Hydroxide (Iron III Hydroxide)
fact: What's usually meant by ‘ferric hydroxide’ is really iron(III) oxide-hydroxide, a reddish-brown gel — and the same compound rust eventually becomes.

name: Zinc Hydroxide
fact: Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric like aluminium's hydroxide: too much of the same lye that precipitates it will turn around and redissolve it as zincate.

name: Lithium Hydroxide
fact: LiOH scrubs carbon dioxide more efficiently pound for pound than any other alkali hydroxide, which is why it's what's stocked on a spacecraft, not sodium hydroxide.

name: Hydroiodic Acid
fact: The strongest of the hydrohalic acids: iodine holds on to its hydrogen more weakly than any other halogen does, so in water it lets go of it most completely.

name: Formic Acid
fact: Named for the Latin for ant — first isolated in 1671 by distilling a large pile of crushed ants, and it's still exactly what a red ant's sting injects.

name: Hydrofluoric Acid
fact: Diluted in water it barely stings on contact — which is exactly what makes it so dangerous: skin damage from a splash can take hours to become obvious.

name: Hydrocyanic Acid
fact: Prussic acid, to the Victorians — a dilute water solution of hydrogen cyanide, lethal at a dose small enough that some people can smell it coming and half can't smell it at all.

name: Methylamine
fact: The simplest amine there is, and it smells distinctly of rotting fish — the smell ammonia takes on once carbon gets involved.

name: Pyridine
fact: A six-membered ring like benzene, but with one carbon swapped for nitrogen — and unlike benzene, it mixes with water in any proportion.

name: Nickel Nitrate
fact: Green crystals from a green solution — nickel salts almost always are. Dissolve the oxide in nitric acid and this is what comes out.

name: Sodium Dichromate
fact: Orange, corrosive, and a confirmed carcinogen -- the hexavalent chromium chemistry behind Hinkley, California's Erin Brockovich case.

name: Tartaric acid
fact: Crystallises out of wine barrels as 'wine stone' — cream of tartar's parent acid.

name: Zinc Iodide
fact: Zinc and iodine won't touch each other dry at room temperature — a drop of water as catalyst is enough to set the reaction boiling.

name: Aluminum Bromide
fact: Aluminium foil dropped into liquid bromine ignites on contact — the same exothermic trick that makes aluminium chloride.

name: Barium Peroxide
fact: Heat barium oxide in air to 500C and it grabs a second oxygen; past 820C it lets go again.

name: Sodium Percarbonate
fact: Soda ash holding a molecule of hydrogen peroxide -- it lets go the moment it hits water, the trick behind oxygen bleach.

name: Nickel Acetate
fact: Nickel's oxide dissolved in vinegar's acid — the same green salt whether it starts from the oxide, the hydroxide or the carbonate.

name: Sodium Sulfite
fact: Sulfur dioxide caught by soda ash before it can escape — the industrial route runs through carbonate rather than the lab's caustic soda.

name: Sodium Thiosulfate
fact: Photographers call it hypo — it dissolves the unexposed silver halide right off a print, fixing the image in place.

name: Acetaldehyde
fact: Your own liver makes this from every drink you take — it's a big part of why a hangover feels like poisoning.

name: Mannitol
fact: Brown seaweed stores up to a fifth of its dry weight as this sugar alcohol — most of the world's supply is still pressed straight out of it.

name: Styrene
fact: Named for storax, the sweetgum resin an apothecary first isolated it from in 1839 — he also watched it slowly turn to hard rubber sitting in a jar.

name: Polystyrene
fact: Eduard Simon's 1839 jar of styrene hardened on its own — air, light and time were the entire recipe for the world's first sample of this.

name: Tetrachloroethylene
fact: Perc, the dry-cleaner's solvent -- chlorine run over hydrocarbons at high heat, and a probable carcinogen.

name: Potassium Iodate
fact: Iodine disproportionates in hot potassium hydroxide — part climbs to iodate, part falls back to iodide, and the iodate is what fortifies salt.

name: Lead Acetate
fact: 'Sugar of lead' — sweet enough that Romans reduced wine in lead pots for the taste, and it poisoned them for exactly that reason.

name: Potassium Thiocyanate
fact: Fuse potassium cyanide with sulfur and the cyanide's lethal reputation mostly stays behind — thiocyanate is a far gentler ion.

name: Maltose
fact: Named for malt, where it was found — beta-amylase clips starch two glucose units at a time and this is what comes off.

name: Dinitrogen Pentoxide
fact: The cleanest lab route skips heat entirely: ozone oxidises nitrogen dioxide straight to this — which then turns around and destroys more ozone.

name: Ferrocyanide
fact: Six cyanide ions clamped so tightly around one iron atom that the complex can barely release any — a cage that traps the danger along with the ion.

name: Potassium Ferrocyanide
fact: Once made by fusing scrap iron with burnt hooves and horn; today built from cyanide and iron instead, then given its potassium.

name: Xenon Difluoride
fact: Seal xenon and fluorine gas in a glass bulb and leave it in sunlight -- even a cloudy day works. No furnace needed.

name: Lead Iodide
fact: The 'golden rain' demonstration: mix dissolved lead and iodide and hexagonal gold crystals fall out as it cools.

name: Bug
fact: A true bug (Hemiptera) skips the pupa stage — its nymph hatches already looking like a wingless adult.

name: Bus
fact: Daimler's 1898 double-decker, one of the first motor buses, put 20 passengers on a car's own drivetrain.

name: Button
fact: Buttons were sewn on as ornaments for centuries before the buttonhole gave them a job to do.

name: CD
fact: 1.2mm of injection-moulded polycarbonate under an aluminium layer thinner than foil, read by a laser.

name: Cereal
fact: Kellogg patented the toasted-flake process in 1891 and had Corn Flakes on shelves under that name by 1895.

name: Chair
fact: Ancient Egyptian chairs were carved wood — the higher your rank, the taller the one you sat in.

name: Circle
fact: Every point on it sits exactly one radius from the centre — the one rule that defines the whole shape.

name: Clown
fact: Joseph Grimaldi painted his face white in the early 1800s, and most clowns still follow the template he set.

name: Comb
fact: Tortoiseshell combs were once common enough that the trade helped push the hawksbill turtle toward extinction.

name: Cookie
fact: Ruth Wakefield's 1930s Toll House recipe expected chopped chocolate to melt into the dough. It held its shape.

name: Cracker
fact: Jonathan Dodgson Carr's 1836 'water biscuit' rolled the same ship's hardtack dough far thinner and saltier.

name: Crayon
fact: Encaustic painters in ancient Egypt bound pigment into hot beeswax millennia before the first wax crayon.

name: Crown
fact: Soft enough to hammer cold and shape without cracking — which is why gold turns up in crowns worldwide.

name: Cup
fact: Most cheap, mass-produced glassware from the mid-1800s on was pressed into a mould, never blown.

name: Cupcake
fact: The name is literal: early cupcakes were baked one to a pottery cup instead of one big cake to a pan.

name: Curtain
fact: England's earliest window coverings were leather panels threaded on iron rods, before wool took over.

name: Diaper
fact: The word named a woven diamond-pattern cloth for three centuries before it ever meant a baby garment.

name: Dinosaur
fact: The first scientifically recognised dinosaur eggs turned up in Mongolia in 1923, confirming a reptile hunch.

name: Door
fact: Before hinges, a door pivoted on a wooden peg turning in a stone socket worn smooth by centuries of swinging.

name: Dolphin
fact: A toothed whale that hunts by sound — clicks focused through a fat-filled 'melon' in the forehead.

name: Doughnut
fact: Deep-fried instead of baked — the hot oil is what browns the crust and cooks the dough through in minutes.

name: Dress
fact: One piece, not two: a bodice stitched to a skirt so the whole garment hangs from the torso together.

name: Dresser
fact: A table built for one job, the toilette, with a mirror bolted or folded into it since the mid-1700s.

name: Drum
fact: A pot with a skin stretched over the mouth — goblet drums like it turn up in Sumerian finds from 1100 BCE.

name: Ear
fact: A cartilage funnel out front, and hair cells deep inside that turn sound into an actual electrical signal.

name: Greasepaint
fact: Zinc-white pigment bound in lard — Carl Baudin's 19th-century stage recipe still underlies clown makeup.

name: Acetone
fact: Fermented, not just distilled — a WWI-era bacterium turned sugar into the acetone cordite production needed.

name: Bisphenol A
fact: Two phenols and one acetone, acid-catalysed together — the 'A' in the name is literally for acetone.

name: Phosgene
fact: The industrial reagent behind a lot of ordinary plastic is also the deadliest gas of the First World War.

name: Polycarbonate
fact: About a billion kilograms of it a year, almost all made by linking BPA into chains with phosgene.

name: Thymol
fact: Thyme's own essential oil, steam-distilled out — once a hookworm treatment, now in mouthwash.

name: Bromothymol Blue
fact: A pH indicator: yellow below 6.0, green near neutral, blue above 7.6.

name: Ammonium Iodide
fact: Ammonia's salt of hydroiodic acid — taken as a dietary supplement when iodine runs short.

name: Ammonium Nitrite
fact: So unstable it is never stored pure — it decomposes to nitrogen gas and water at room temperature.

name: Bromate
fact: BrO3-, a suspected carcinogen strict enough to have forced a UK recall of bottled water.

name: Dinitrogen Trioxide
fact: N2O3, deep blue as a liquid or solid — but stable only below -21°C before it falls back apart.

name: Ethylene Oxide
fact: Reactive enough to sterilise a hospital's plastic syringes — carcinogenic for the same reason.

name: Ethylene Glycol
fact: Sweet enough to poison a pet that finds it first — the antifreeze that drops water's freezing point by 45°C.

name: Nickel Sulfate
fact: Turquoise crystals, and the single most common cause of a positive nickel-allergy patch test.

name: Iodide
fact: Iodine reduced by one electron — the form the human thyroid actually takes it up in.

name: Potassium Sulfite
fact: E225. First isolated in the early 1700s, and known for a while as Stahl's sulphureous salt.

name: Silver Carbonate
fact: Precipitates colourless and turns yellow within minutes — nothing about it stays as first made.

name: Sodium Amide
fact: A base strong enough to pull a proton straight off an alkyne — and violent with water.

name: Sodium Nitride
fact: Falls back apart into sodium metal and nitrogen gas almost as readily as it is made.

name: Sodium Cyanide
fact: The salt that dissolves gold straight out of crushed ore — and a dose under a gram can be fatal.

name: Strontium Nitrate
fact: Burns pure enough to give fireworks and road flares their deep, characteristic red.

name: Bleach
fact: Chlorine gas run into cold lye — the industrial route behind nearly every bottle sold as bleach.

name: Aluminium Fluoride
fact: Stirred into molten alumina, it drops the smelting bath's melting point by over 1,000°C.

name: Butanoic Acid
fact: Rancid butter's exact smell — dogs catch it at 10 parts per billion, far below what people notice.

name: Lithium Carbonate
fact: Tarnish lithium leaves in damp air — and, separately, a mood stabiliser shown to cut suicide risk by 87%.

name: Lithium Phosphate
fact: What precipitates out feeds straight into lithium iron phosphate battery cathodes.

name: Hypobromous Acid
fact: The compound that actually does the disinfecting in a bromine-treated hot tub.

name: Hypoiodous Acid
fact: As hypoiodite, the oxidiser your own white blood cells make to use iodine as a weapon on pathogens.

name: Rhyolite
fact: Granite's chemistry, chilled fast at the surface — the most silica-rich lava there is.

name: Andesite
fact: Named for the Andes. Its silica content is close to the average of Earth's whole continental crust.

name: Dacite
fact: The rock that domed up in Mount St. Helens's crater after 1980: lava too viscous to flow far.

name: Diorite
fact: Granite and gabbro's compositional midpoint -- a coarse-grained igneous rock the Ancient Egyptians prized for hard, dark statuary that granite tools alone could barely shape.

name: Gabbro
fact: Basalt's slow-cooled twin: same melt, same minerals, just given time to grow visible crystals.

name: Syenite
fact: Almost granite, but the melt ran out of free silica before quartz could form. Named for Syene, old Aswan.

name: Peridotite
fact: Over 40% olivine — the commonest rock in Earth's mantle, and diamond's ride up from in kimberlite.

name: Dunite
fact: Over 90% olivine, peridotite taken almost as far as it goes. Named in 1859 for Dun Mountain, New Zealand.

name: Komatiite
fact: Lava so hot — up to 1,600°C — it flowed like water. Nearly all of it is Archean, laid down when Earth's mantle ran hotter.

name: Anorthosite
fact: 90–100% plagioclase feldspar, floated together because it's lighter than the melt around it. The Moon's highlands are the same rock.

name: Pegmatite
fact: Granite's minerals given a watery, low-viscosity residue to grow in. A pegmatite beryl crystal from Madagascar reached 18 metres.

name: Perlite
fact: Obsidian that absorbed water over geologic time. Flash-heated past 850°C, the trapped water turns to steam and it puffs up to 16x its size.

name: Tuff
fact: Compacted volcanic ash, soft enough to carve. Rome's Servian Wall and every moai on Easter Island are cut from it.

name: Xenolith
fact: A chunk of older rock, swallowed whole by rising magma before it could melt — a free sample of rock from miles underground.

name: Porphyry
fact: Big crystals frozen mid-growth in a much finer matrix. Rome reserved a deep purple variety, quarried in Egypt, for emperors alone.

name: Potassium Chlorate
fact: KClO3. A powerful oxidizer — the sensitizer packed into a match head, not the strip it's struck against.

name: Hypochlorite
fact: ClO⁻. Chlorine dumped into cold lye disproportionates into this and plain chloride, all in one step.

name: Hydrazine
fact: N2H4. Reacts with certain oxidizers on contact, no spark needed — why spacecraft thrusters run on it.

name: Acetamide
fact: Vinegar's acid with an amide swapped in for the -OH. Molten, it dissolves almost anything.

name: Sodium Silicate
fact: Water glass. Sand fused with an alkali gives a syrupy solution that bonds cardboard and detergent granules.

name: Potassium Chromate
fact: K2CrO4, bright yellow. One roasting step turns chromium's harmless green oxide hexavalent.

name: Zinc Sulfate
fact: ZnSO4. A dietary supplement, a fungicide and a textile mordant, all the same white zinc salt.

name: Chromic Acid
fact: H2CrO4 in solution. Acidify a chromate far enough and it protonates all the way to this.

name: Methyl Acetate
fact: The smallest common ester of acetic acid — fruity, fast-evaporating nail polish remover base.

name: Dimethyl Sulfide
fact: The sulfur smell of the sea and of boiled cabbage. Algae make it by the megatonne.

name: Dimethyl Sulfoxide
fact: DMSO. Crosses skin so readily that whatever is dissolved in it comes along for the ride.

name: Hexane
fact: C6H14. Boils at 69°C, the window refiners cut it out of crude oil in to leach oil from soybeans.

name: Eugenol
fact: 72 to 90 percent of clove oil is this one molecule — most of why cloves smell the way they do.

name: Potassium Bitartrate
fact: Cream of tartar. Crystallizes out of grape juice as it ferments — "wine diamonds" in the cask.

name: Sodium Potassium Tartrate
fact: Rochelle salt — one of the first materials found to be piezoelectric, making its own voltage.

name: Hexamine
fact: Methenamine. Burns clean, no soot or puddled fuel — why camp stoves use little tablets of it.

name: Phosphorus Pentachloride
fact: PCl5. Reacts violently with water, tearing itself back apart into phosphoric acid and hydrochloric acid.

name: Potassium Oxide
fact: K2O. Fertilizer labels report potassium content as if it were all this, though barely any is.

name: Potassium Phosphate
fact: E340. A sodium-free stand-in for trisodium phosphate, buffering cereal, sauce and cheese pH.

name: Silver Acetate
fact: Silver paired with vinegar's acid. In gum or lozenges, it turns smoke metallic-tasting to deter smokers.

name: Ankle
fact: A hinge where the shin bones meet the talus — the only true mortise-and-tenon joint in the body.

name: Arm
fact: Humerus above the elbow, radius and ulna below, muscle wrapped around all three.

name: Baby
fact: Newborn to about age one — 'infant', before the word has to share the job with anything else.

name: Bag
fact: Cloth or hide folded at the edges and cinched shut with a cord of the same fibre.

name: Bagel
fact: Boiled 60 to 90 seconds before it ever sees an oven. That's the whole trick.

name: Backpack
fact: A bag that traded its drawstring for two straps and moved the load onto the shoulders.

name: Balloon
fact: Michael Faraday made the first rubber ones in 1824 — to hold hydrogen for lectures, not parties.

name: Ball
fact: Mesoamerican players whipped latex with morning-glory vine sap — sticky sap, turned into real bounce.

name: Barn
fact: Old English for 'barley house'. The job never changed: keep the harvest dry.

name: Baseball Bat
fact: Turned on a lathe from one solid billet — ash for a century, maple since 1997.

name: Bathtub
fact: Kohler's foundry enamelled cast-iron horse troughs after an 1880 fire. Flip the ears into a rim.

name: Bed
fact: Medieval mattresses were wool, feathers or hair stuffed onto a wood frame, off the drafty floor.

name: Belt
fact: Leather bends, folds and cinches tight without tearing — why it beat cloth as the standard strap.

name: Bird
fact: Feathers and a toothless, horn-covered beak, on every one of the roughly 11,000 living species.

name: Blanket
fact: Wool is the classic fill — thick, warm cloth on its own, long before cotton or synthetics joined in.

name: Building Block
fact: Birch takes a fine, splinter-free polish once it's sanded — safe corners for a toddler's hands.

name: Boot
fact: The only real difference from a shoe is height: enough leather to cover the ankle, sometimes the knee.

name: Bowl
fact: A calabash gourd, dried hard and split in half. Most of the world used exactly this before pottery.

name: Bridge
fact: A clapper bridge is nothing but a flat slab of stone laid across two piers — engineering by omission.

name: Broom
fact: A besom: twigs bound to a handle. English kept the name long after brooms stopped being the plant.

name: Brush
fact: Fibres tied to a handle — split palm leaf in ancient Egypt, plant fibre or animal hair ever since.

name: Bubble
fact: Soap cuts water's surface tension enough for a puff of air to stretch it a micrometre thin.

name: Bucket
fact: A cooper's trade scaled down: staves bent into a cylinder, cinched tight with a metal hoop.

name: Dwarf Planet
fact: Round under its own gravity like a planet, but it hasn't cleared its neighbourhood — the 2006 line.

name: Kuiper Belt
fact: A disc of icy bodies beyond Neptune, running from about 30 out to 50 astronomical units.

name: Oort Cloud
fact: A shell of icy leftovers flung outward by the giant planets, reaching perhaps 100,000 AU from the Sun.

name: Great Dark Spot
fact: A storm on Neptune the size of Earth, photographed by Voyager 2 in 1989 — and gone by 1994.

name: Tidal Locking
fact: Why the Moon always shows Earth the same face — nobody saw the far side until 1959.

name: Solar Wind
fact: Charged particles streaming off the Sun's corona, stripping thin atmospheres like Mars's away.

name: Lima Bean
fact: Phaseolus lunatus, a species apart from the common bean — domesticated in the Peruvian Andes around 2000 BC.

name: Black-Eyed Pea
fact: Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea — domesticated in Africa and bred to thrive in soil up to 85% sand.

name: Navy Bean
fact: A small white cultivar of the common bean, named for the US Navy's use of it as a sailor's ration.

name: Pine Nut
fact: Not cracked from a shell like other nuts — shaken loose from a cone dried until it splits open.

name: Brazil Nut
fact: Rarely farmed — plantation trees seldom fruit, since few bee genera can pollinate the flower.

name: Almond Butter
fact: Almonds, crushed to a spreadable paste the same way peanuts are for peanut butter.

name: Marzipan
fact: Ground almonds worked with sugar until pliable enough to shape by hand — documented in Toledo back to 1512.

name: Pumpkin Seed
fact: Sold hulled as pepitas, or whole in a white husk — some cultivars are bred huskless from the start.

name: Soy Milk
fact: Soaked soybeans, ground with water, boiled 15 to 20 minutes, then strained — the liquid tofu is curdled from.

name: Tempeh
fact: Whole soybeans, not curdled like tofu — a mould's mycelium binds the beans into a cake in about a day.

name: Edamame
fact: Soybeans picked green, 35 to 40 days after the plant flowers — sweeter than they'll ever be once dried.

name: Green Bean
fact: The same species as kidney and pinto beans, picked immature and eaten pod and all — a fresh legume.

name: Falafel
fact: Ground raw, not cooked first — cooked chickpeas fall apart in the fryer instead of holding together.

name: Refried Beans
fact: Frijoles refritos — ‘well fried,’ not fried twice. Mashed pinto beans, fried in fat until they hold together.

name: Dal
fact: Names both the raw split pulse and the dish — lentils cooked down soft, a staple across South Asia.

name: Hoppin' John
fact: Black-eyed peas and rice, eaten across the US South on New Year's Day — the peas stand in for coins.

name: Boston Baked Beans
fact: Colonial New England swapped molasses and salt pork into a Native bean-pit method once run on bear fat.

name: Propylene
fact: The propene molecule — steam-cracked from petroleum alongside ethylene, its own biggest use is polypropylene.

name: 1,3-Butadiene
fact: A four-carbon diene pulled from the same steam-cracker stream as ethylene — the monomer synthetic rubber runs on.

name: Acrylonitrile
fact: CH2=CHCN. Ammoxidized from propylene by the Sohio process — the nitrile in nitrile rubber and in PAN fiber.

name: Nitrile Rubber (NBR)
fact: A butadiene-acrylonitrile copolymer, oil-resistant enough to be the standard glove and fuel-line rubber.

name: Chloromethane
fact: CH3Cl, also called methyl chloride — hydrochlorinated from methanol, and the feedstock silicone starts from.

name: Dimethyldichlorosilane
fact: Me2SiCl2 — the direct-process product that almost every industrial silicone is hydrolyzed from.

name: Silicone (VMQ)
fact: A silicon-oxygen backbone with organic side groups — polydimethylsiloxane, stable from caulk to breast implants.

name: Aniline
fact: C6H5NH2. Made from nitrobenzene or, less commonly, straight from phenol and ammonia.

name: Isocyanate
fact: The R-N=C=O group, built by phosgenating an amine — the reactive half of every polyurethane.

name: Polyol
fact: A multi-hydroxyl molecule built by ring-opening an alkylene oxide onto a starter alcohol like glycerol.

name: Polyurethane (PU)
fact: A diisocyanate and a polyol, stitched together into carbamate links — foam cushions to skateboard wheels.

name: Inconel 625
fact: A nickel-chromium-molybdenum superalloy that keeps its strength red-hot — jet engines, chemical plant, seabed risers.

name: Borosilicate Glass
fact: Silica and boric oxide melted together — the low-expansion glass that survives a hot pan going into cold water.

name: Silicon Carbide (SiC)
fact: SiC — Acheson's 1893 furnace product, almost as hard as diamond and sold as an abrasive under the name carborundum.

name: Zirconia (ZrO2)
fact: Zirconium dioxide — ceramic-hard, cut as a diamond simulant, and stable enough for dental crowns and oxygen sensors.

name: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN)
fact: Free-radically polymerized from acrylonitrile — spun into filament yarn as the precursor for 90% of carbon fiber.

name: Carbon Fiber
fact: PAN fiber stabilized in air and then carbonized past 1,000°C, driving off everything that isn't carbon.

name: Epichlorohydrin
fact: A chlorinated epoxide — made from propylene or, in Dow's newer process, straight from glycerol and HCl.

name: Epoxy Resin
fact: Bisphenol A stepped together with epichlorohydrin into DGEBA — the resin behind most structural adhesives.

name: Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP)
fact: Carbon fiber laid into a resin matrix, usually epoxy — strong along the fiber, and a fraction of steel's weight.

name: Glass Fiber
fact: Molten glass drawn through a spinneret's tiny holes into continuous filament — fine enough to weave.

name: Fiberglass (GFRP)
fact: Glass fiber set into a plastic matrix — epoxy, polyester or vinyl ester — cheap, stiff, and everywhere from boat hulls to bathtubs.

name: Wood Flour
fact: Sawdust and wood waste ground fine enough to feel like sand — the filler in wood-plastic decking.

name: Wood-Plastic Composite (WPC)
fact: Wood flour compounded into a thermoplastic, usually polyethylene — decking that won't rot or splinter.

name: POM (Acetal / Delrin)
fact: Polyoxymethylene — formaldehyde strung into long -CH2O- chains, stiff and low-friction enough to replace metal gears.

name: PPS (Polyphenylene Sulfide)
fact: [C6H4S]n — a benzene ring and a sulfur atom, repeated, and one of the few plastics that shrugs off 200°C.

name: EPDM
fact: An ethylene-propylene-diene terpolymer that resists ozone and weather better than almost any other rubber.

name: Chervil
fact: A parsley relative with a faint anise taste — one of the four French fines herbes.

name: Lemongrass
fact: A tropical grass, not a citrus — its lemon smell is geraniol and citronellol, straight from the leaf oil.

name: Savory
fact: A mint-family annual, prized with beans across Persian, Georgian and Balkan kitchens.

name: Anise
fact: Carrot's own family, not star anise's — the two plants share only a flavour compound, by coincidence.

name: Shallot
fact: An onion cultivar that grows in clustered offsets like garlic, not from one bulb — and tastes milder for it.

name: Scallion
fact: An onion pulled before its bulb ever forms — the same plant, kept for its hollow green stem instead.

name: Garlic Chives
fact: A different Allium species from common chives — flat leaves, and a taste closer to garlic than onion.

name: White Pepper
fact: The same peppercorn as black pepper, ripe instead of unripe, with the rotted-off skin never dried on.

name: Green Peppercorn
fact: The same vine's unripe fruit, brined before it can darken — sharper and fresher than the dried kind.

name: Cayenne
fact: The same species as sweet paprika, bred and picked for capsaicin instead of colour.

name: Celery Seed
fact: Not a seed but a whole dried fruit, off the same plant grown elsewhere for its stalk.

name: Mace
fact: The lacy red aril wrapped around a nutmeg seed, peeled off and dried into its own spice.

name: Chili Powder
fact: A ground blend of dried chilies with cumin, garlic and onion — not chili pepper alone.

name: Chestnut
fact: Unrelated to the toxic horse chestnut despite the name — its spiny bur splits open once ripe on its own.

name: Sunflower Seed
fact: Striped seeds are the snack type — the solid black-hulled kind goes to the oil press instead.

name: Balsamic Vinegar
fact: Not soured wine at all — boiled-down grape must, aged in wood for a legal minimum of 12 years.

name: Sesame Oil
fact: Pressed from roasted rather than raw seed — what gives toasted sesame oil its deep amber colour.

name: Steak Sauce
fact: A ketchup-style base fortified with extra vinegar and spice — tangier than ketchup by design.

name: Relish
fact: Pickle, chopped small enough to spread rather than slice — same preservation, different knife work.

name: Bouquet Garni
fact: French for 'garnished bouquet' — herbs tied in a bundle so they can be fished back out of the pot.

name: Marinade
fact: Acid, oil and spice in balance — too much acid toughens meat instead of tenderising it.

name: Chloroform
fact: CHCl3 -- once a surgical anaesthetic, now a suspected carcinogen and an ozone-depleting solvent.

name: Chlorodifluoromethane
fact: R-22, the refrigerant gas that cooled most 20th-century air conditioners and freezers.

name: Tetrafluoroethylene
fact: TFE -- the monomer for Teflon, discovered by accident in 1938 when a cylinder of it polymerised on its own.

name: PTFE
fact: Teflon. A carbon backbone wrapped entirely in fluorine -- almost nothing sticks to it or dissolves it.

name: Hexafluoropropylene
fact: HFP -- TFE's own high-heat byproduct, and the second monomer in most fluoroelastomers.

name: PFA
fact: Perfluoroalkoxy alkane -- almost pure PTFE chemistry, but able to melt-process instead of only sintering.

name: FKM
fact: Viton. A fluoroelastomer o-ring seal that shrugs off fuel, oil and heat that would swell ordinary rubber.

name: Ethylidene Chloride
fact: 1,1-Dichloroethane -- a Lewis-acid-catalysed addition of HCl across vinyl chloride's double bond.

name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane
fact: Once sold as 'chlorothene', a huge industrial solvent until its ozone damage got it phased out.

name: Chlorodifluoroethane
fact: HCFC-142b -- a refrigerant gas whose whole purpose, industrially, is to be cracked into something else.

name: Vinylidene Fluoride
fact: VDF, CH2=CF2 -- the monomer shared by PVDF plastic and Viton-family fluoroelastomers.

name: PVDF
fact: Kynar. Half its hydrogens replaced with fluorine, which is enough to make it piezoelectric.

name: CFC-113
fact: 1,1,2-Trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane -- a Montreal Protocol chemical, once everywhere as a degreaser.

name: Chlorotrifluoroethylene
fact: CTFE -- one chlorine short of tetrafluoroethylene, and the monomer half of ECTFE.

name: ECTFE
fact: Halar. Ethylene and chlorotrifluoroethylene alternating almost perfectly, one after the other, down the chain.

name: Ethylene Dichloride
fact: EDC, 1,2-dichloroethane -- made and cracked again in the same plant, on the way to vinyl chloride.

name: Vinyl Chloride
fact: VCM -- a known human carcinogen, and the monomer that makes up every molecule of PVC.

name: PVC
fact: Polyvinyl chloride. The vinyl chloride monomer is a genuine carcinogen; the finished plastic is not.

name: LDPE
fact: Low-density polyethylene -- branched, flexible chains, the plastic of bags and squeeze bottles and film.

name: UHMWPE
fact: Chains millions of daltons long -- too long to melt cleanly, so it goes into hip joints instead.

name: PP
fact: Polypropylene -- the second most produced plastic on Earth, and the one hinges best without snapping.

name: Butane
fact: Discovered in crude petroleum in 1864 -- the lightest liquid fraction, condensing at just above 0°C.

name: Polybutadiene
fact: Synthetic rubber, chosen for tire treads for the same bounce natural rubber has and steadier supply.

name: Styrene-Acrylonitrile
fact: SAN -- clear and rigid on its own, and the resin half of ABS before rubber gets grafted in.

name: ABS
fact: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene -- the plastic LEGO bricks, keyboard caps and car dashboards are made of.

name: Xylene
fact: A three-carbon step up from toluene -- three isomers, and the para one becomes polyester.

name: Terephthalic Acid
fact: p-Xylene's two methyl groups oxidised to acids -- the feedstock behind nearly all polyester.

name: PET
fact: Polyethylene terephthalate -- soda bottles and polyester fibre are the same molecule, spun or blown.

name: Hydroquinone
fact: Two hydroxyls on opposite corners of a benzene ring -- a photographic developer and a skin-lightening agent.

name: Nitrobenzene
fact: Smells of almonds, looks pale yellow, and is toxic enough that its main use is becoming something else.

name: Fluoroboric Acid
fact: HBF4 -- boric acid dissolved straight into hydrofluoric acid, four fluorines clamping onto one boron.

name: Benzenediazonium Chloride
fact: An aniline salt so unstable it is explosive dry -- made cold and used within the hour.

name: Benzenediazonium Tetrafluoroborate
fact: Swap the chloride's counterion for tetrafluoroborate and the same unstable salt becomes shock-insensitive.

name: Fluorobenzene
fact: A benzene ring with one hydrogen swapped for fluorine -- the Balz-Schiemann reaction's signature product.

name: 4,4'-Difluorobenzophenone
fact: Two fluorinated benzene rings joined through a ketone -- one of PEEK's two building-block monomers.

name: PEEK
fact: Polyetheretherketone -- keeps its strength past 250°C, used in jet engines and spinal implants.

name: Cyclohexanone
fact: A six-carbon ring with one carbon turned into a ketone -- 'KA oil', the doorway to nylon.

name: Hydroxylamine
fact: NH2OH -- explosive as a pure solid, so it is made, used and consumed as a dilute solution instead.

name: Cyclohexanone Oxime
fact: Cyclohexanone's oxygen swapped for a nitrogen -- one rearrangement away from a ring nylon is made of.

name: Caprolactam
fact: A seven-membered ring, waiting to be forced open into the single long chain of nylon 6.

name: Nylon 6
fact: Every unit is the same caprolactam ring, unlike nylon 6,6's two alternating monomers.

name: Potassium Carbonate
fact: K2CO3, potash — named for literally being ash boiled down in a pot, the alkali that came before purified lye.

name: Sodium Oxide
fact: Na2O — sodium's true oxide, easily overshot to the peroxide if there's oxygen to spare.

name: Zinc Nitrate
fact: Zn(NO3)2 — dissolve zinc in nitric acid and this crystallises out, one of six water molecules still attached.

name: Phthalic Anhydride
fact: C6H4(CO)2O — nearly all of it today comes off a xylene flame, not the naphthalene it was first made from.

name: Phenolphthalein
fact: The lab's own mood ring — colourless below pH 8.2, hot pink above it, and that's the entire instrument.

name: Magnesium Nitrate
fact: Mg(NO3)2 — a magnesium salt so eager for water it's used industrially to pull the last of it out of concentrated nitric acid.

name: Ammonium Acetate
fact: NH4CH3CO2 — so hygroscopic it's nearly impossible to keep dry, and it breaks back down toward acetic acid and ammonia if melted.

name: Bicarbonate
fact: HCO3- — carbon dioxide's most common disguise in blood and seawater alike, the form that actually carries most of it around.

name: Chromate
fact: CrO4(2-) — chromium at its most oxidised, +6, the state that turns ore green going in and this colour coming out.

name: Methyl Ethyl Ketone
fact: Butanone, MEK — nail-polish-remover-sharp, and one of the few common solvents that dissolves both polar and non-polar compounds at once.

name: Trichloroacetic Acid
fact: CCl3CO2H — three chlorines pull so much electron density off the acid group that it's a stronger acid than sulfuric, dose for dose.

name: Magnesium Sulfate
fact: MgSO4 — Epsom salt, named for a Surrey spring, and the same compound used in hospital drips to stop premature labour.

name: Sulfur Trioxide
fact: SO3 — the molecule sulfuric acid is built from, and so hungry for water it fumes visibly in ordinary damp air.

name: Aluminum Phosphate
fact: AlPO4 — aluminium and phosphate combine in nearly the same one-to-one ratio silicon and oxygen do in quartz, which is why its frameworks mimic zeolites.

name: Stearic Acid
fact: The straight 18-carbon fatty acid that makes tallow solid at room temperature, and candle wax firm instead of greasy.

name: Dinitrogen Monoxide
fact: N2O — the anaesthetic gas dentists call laughing gas, one nitrogen short of the nitrite it takes two more oxidation steps to reach.

name: Acetonitrile
fact: CH3CN — the smallest nitrile, and mostly a byproduct: burned off from the plant that makes acrylonitrile rather than made on purpose.

name: Potassium Dichromate
fact: K2Cr2O7 — the orange crystal that gave 19th-century chemistry its favourite oxidiser, before hexavalent chromium's cancer risk was understood.

name: Zinc Acetate
fact: Zn(CH3CO2)2 — zinc's salt of vinegar's acid, and the zinc source dropped into throat lozenges and cold remedies.

name: Magnesium Carbonate
fact: MgCO3, magnesite — limestone's magnesium twin, and the mineral a chunk of gym chalk is mostly made of.

name: Propane
