fact: Three carbons, sold compressed in the tank by the house. Boils at −42°C, below any winter night.

name: Pentane
fact: Five carbons, and the shortest alkane that's a true liquid at room temperature rather than a compressed gas.

name: Octane
fact: Eight carbons, and fuel quality's own ruler — the 100 on an octane rating is defined against its branched cousin.

name: Benzene
fact: A six-carbon ring so stable Kekulé is said to have dreamed its shape as a snake biting its own tail.

name: Hydrobromic Acid
fact: Hydrogen bromide dissolved in water — a strong acid with a lower profile than its chlorine cousin.

name: Carbonic Acid
fact: What CO2 becomes the instant it meets water — the fizz in soda, and half of blood's pH control.

name: Ammonium Sulfate
fact: 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, and it acidifies alkaline soil as it feeds it — two fertiliser jobs in one salt.

name: Copper Sulfate
fact: Blue vitriol. Painted onto grapevines as Bordeaux mixture since 1885, still farming’s default fungicide.

name: Sulfurous Acid
fact: SO2 dissolved in water — so unstable it has never been isolated pure, only ever as this equilibrium.

name: Galactose
fact: Glucose's mirror-twin, locked to it inside every molecule of milk sugar until digestion pulls them apart.

name: Sodium Nitrate
fact: Chile saltpetre — nitrogen mined from Atacama desert crusts a metre thick, never having had to fix itself.

name: Iodic Acid
fact: HIO3 — corrosive like any acid, and a strong enough oxidiser to be a fire hazard around anything combustible.

name: Camphor
fact: That mothball smell, once drawn only from a tree's wood, before chemists learned to build it from turpentine.

name: Silver Iodide
fact: A handful of grains seeded into a cloud can nudge a snowflake into forming around them instead of dust.

name: Arsenic Trioxide
fact: White arsenic — Victorian fiction's classic poison, and today a treatment for a rare form of leukaemia.

name: Gold(III) Oxide
fact: Gold's rarer oxide, and a reluctant one — heat it past 298°C and it falls back apart into the metal.

name: Gold Sulfide
fact: Gold refusing to stay dissolved: pass the right gas through a gold salt solution and this drops out of it.

name: Turpentine
fact: Pine resin steam-distilled down to a solvent — the smell in old paint tins, before petroleum replaced it.

name: Lactose
fact: Milk's own sugar, crystallised straight out of cheesemaking's leftover whey.

name: Wire
fact: Any ductile metal, pulled cold through a die until it's thin enough to bend by hand.

name: Battery
fact: A zinc can for a shell and a manganese dioxide paste inside — the dry cell that made power portable.

name: Skin
fact: Two layers, two jobs: keratin-packed epidermis for a barrier, collagen-rich dermis underneath for strength.

name: Ligament
fact: The same dense collagen bundle as a tendon — a tendon ties muscle to bone, a ligament ties bone to bone.

name: Earring
fact: Gold hammered thin and bent into a hoop — the oldest known earrings, from Ur, are about 4,500 years old.

name: Elbow
fact: A hinge joint of three bones — humerus, radius, ulna — held together by a ligament on either side.

name: Envelope
fact: Paper cut and folded into a rhombus, kite or cross, its overlapping flap held down with a dab of gum.

name: Eye
fact: The retina isn't just wired to the brain — developmentally it is brain tissue, budded outward before birth.

name: Fence
fact: Wire strands stretched taut between wooden posts — far less timber than a fence built solid.

name: Fingernail
fact: A flattened claw: primate nails evolved from ancestral claws to back a sensitive fingertip pad.

name: Finger
fact: Bones called phalanges — three to a finger, two to a thumb — wrapped in skin at a hand's working end.

name: Fire Truck
fact: A combustion engine bolted to a hose and pump — motorised fire engines started replacing horses around 1897.

name: Flashlight
fact: David Misell's 1899 patent: dry-cell batteries in a paper tube, with a bulb and brass reflector at the end.

name: Fork
fact: Common in Byzantium by the 4th century, still mocked as an Italian affectation in 18th-century England.

name: Garbage Can
fact: A steel bin coated in zinc — the same galvanising that keeps an outdoor nail or bucket from rusting through.

name: Ghost
fact: No sighting has been reproduced under controlled conditions; psychologists point to pareidolia instead.

name: Glasses
fact: First ground in Pisa or Florence around 1290; wire temples over the ears took four more centuries.

name: Glove
fact: Sheepskin turned inside out keeps its own wool fleece attached — a glove and its lining from one hide.

name: Glue
fact: Boiled from hide instead of bone, the same collagen chemistry as gelatin — just dried coarse, not refined.

name: Goal
fact: Football had no goal net until 1889 — before that, a disputed score meant arguing about where the ball went.

name: Hair
fact: Keratin filament grown from a follicle in the skin — only the root is alive, never the shaft you can see.

name: Hanger
fact: One length of wire, bent into a triangle and a hook — most coat hangers today are still just steel wire.

name: Hat
fact: Felted fur or wool, stitched and stretched to shape — a fedora is just a soft felt hat with a creased crown.

name: Head
fact: The skull is a bony case built entirely around the brain it protects, with one hinge left for the jaw.

name: Hoop
fact: Naismith nailed up a peach basket in 1891; by 1906 an open metal rim let the ball just pass through.

name: Hose
fact: Rubber wrapped around a woven fabric core — the reinforcement is what keeps it from bursting under pressure.

name: Spring
fact: Steel wound into a coil, then hardened and tempered so it remembers its shape and snaps back after a bend.

name: Slinky
fact: 98 coils of spring steel — the gauge Richard James found, after a year of testing, that would walk downstairs.

name: Sock
fact: Oldest knitted finds: 11th-century cotton socks from Fustat, near Cairo — knitting stretches to fit a foot.

name: Carbonated Water
fact: Joseph Priestley dissolved CO2 into water above a Leeds brewery vat in 1767, his self-declared 'happiest' find.

name: Soda
fact: Mostly carbonated water: commercial cola syrup is cut roughly one part syrup to five parts carbonated water.

name: Sofa
fact: A wood frame under padding, covered in leather or fabric — the Chesterfield's buttoned look dates to the 1700s.

name: Spider Web
fact: Pure silk protein from spinneret glands — a web is commonly about 20 times the size of the spider that spun it.

name: Spoon
fact: A reindeer-antler spoon from the Magdalenian, some 17,000 years old, carves the idea wood spoons still use.

name: Squirrel
fact: A scatter-hoarder that buries several thousand acorns, seeds and nuts a season, and mostly finds them again.

name: Stairs
fact: Cut straight into rock at Egypt's Red Pyramid around 2575 BC — the steps were the material itself, nothing added.

name: Stick
fact: The smallest branches on a tree are twigs — already its driest, most brittle wood, first to snap off in wind.

name: Sticker
fact: Hide glue and gelatin are one substance under two names — boiled collagen, stiff enough to bind paper down.

name: Stove
fact: The first cast-iron stove was built in 1642 at Lynn, Massachusetts — an iron box, with no grates yet.

name: Postage Stamp
fact: The Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp, went on sale 1 May 1840 — paper gummed with starch paste.

name: Stool
fact: One of the earliest forms of wooden furniture — ancient Greece's diphros even folded flat to travel.

name: String
fact: One more twist than thread, one fewer than rope — plied against its own twist so it cannot unravel.

name: Suitcase
fact: Early suitcases stretched leather over a rigid wood-or-steel frame, with leather or brass caps at the corners.

name: Sunglasses
fact: Ai Tai, 'dark clouds': flat panes of smoky quartz worn in 12th-century China, said to hide judges' expressions.

name: Sweater
fact: The word dates only to 1882, first a woolen vest worn rowing — unscoured wool keeps lanolin and sheds water.

name: Swimsuit
fact: Before the 1930s, swimsuits were wool — they never hugged the body and turned heavy the moment they got wet.

name: Swing
fact: The simplest playground swing needs nothing but a rope over a branch and a seat tied to the ends.

name: Table
fact: Ancient Egyptian tables, around 2500 BC, were wood and alabaster; medieval trestle tables folded away after meals.

name: Tape
fact: Richard Drew's 1925 masking tape was paper backed with a gentler rubber adhesive, made for autobody painters.

name: Teapot
fact: China's shift from whipped tea to steeped leaves called the teapot into being; the earliest one dates to 1513.

name: Nose
fact: The nose's shape is mostly cartilage, not bone — only the bridge is bony — wrapped in skin that's thinnest at the tip.

name: Olfactory Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve I: fibers rise from the nasal lining through the ethmoid bone's cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb.

name: Optic Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve II carries vision from retina to brain — and is technically CNS tissue, not a true peripheral nerve.

name: Trigeminal Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve V: three branches carry sensation from the whole face, and its motor branch alone powers chewing.

name: Vestibulocochlear Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve VIII fuses hearing and balance in one sheath: a cochlear branch for sound, vestibular for motion.

name: Vagus Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve X, named for 'wandering': its right branch reaches the heart's own pacemaker to slow the beat.

name: Accessory Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve XI drives two muscles: sternocleidomastoid, which turns the head, and trapezius, which shrugs it.

name: Hypoglossal Nerve
fact: Cranial nerve XII: purely motor, it alone drives the tongue's own muscles for speech, chewing, and swallowing.

name: Durian
fact: Named for duri, Malay for thorn. The smell strong enough to get it banned from hotels and transit is organosulfur chemistry — diethyl disulfide, dimethyl sulfide and more, the same family that makes onion and garlic sharp.

name: Lavender
fact: A Mediterranean shrub grown for its flower spikes. Nearly all of its scent is one molecule, linalool — lavender oil is the reference chemists compare other linalool-scented things to.

name: Caraway
fact: Carum carvi, Apiaceae like cumin and dill — so alike to cumin that many languages don't bother separating them. Its root is also a genuine root vegetable, eaten like a parsnip.

name: Elderflower
fact: The flowerhead of Sambucus nigra, picked before it sets fruit and steeped for cordial — the one part of the elder that needs no cooking to be safe.

name: Oyster Leaf
fact: Mertensia maritima, a shingle-beach succulent from the Arctic fringe of the Northern Hemisphere. Chewed raw, it genuinely tastes like an oyster.

name: Fenugreek
fact: A legume, family to peas and beans, grown for both its seed and its leaf. The seed carries sotolon, the same molecule behind curry, maple syrup and aged sherry's burnt-sugar edge.

name: Paracress
fact: Acmella oleracea — toothache plant, buzz buttons, electric daisy. Its own name for the tingling, numbing jolt in the flower bud is spilanthol.

name: Yuzu
fact: A hybrid of mandarin and the wild ichang papeda, and it inherited that parent's cold tolerance — yuzu survives winters down to -7°C that would kill an ordinary orange tree.

name: Wakame
fact: Undaria pinnatifida, the same order as kelp — Laminariales — grown by Japanese and Korean sea-farmers for centuries. Not a plant at all: a brown-algal stramenopile.

name: Capsaicin
fact: Chilli's heat, and it barely dissolves in water — 0.0013 g per 100 mL — which is why milk cuts the burn and water does not.

name: Benzaldehyde
fact: Almond-scented in savoury use, cherry-scented in sweet — the same molecule read differently by context. Water hitting a crushed apricot kernel's amygdalin makes it, along with hydrogen cyanide.

name: Allyl Isothiocyanate
fact: Undetectable until the plant is damaged — an enzyme called myrosinase only meets its target molecule, sinigrin, once cells rupture. Then mustard, wasabi and horseradish all sting the same way.

name: Nootkatone
fact: Present in only trace amounts, but it is grapefruit's single most valuable aroma compound.

name: Nonadienal
fact: (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal, often just called cucumber aldehyde — the compound so tied to the vegetable it doubles as the name.

name: Filbertone
fact: The hazelnut's own character-impact compound — no other nut carries it, which is why nothing else quite smells like one.

name: Isoamyl Acetate
fact: Also called banana oil, and used to flavour banana candy for exactly that reason — it occurs naturally in the ripe fruit itself, among dozens of other aroma molecules.

name: Sotolon
fact: Fenugreek's main flavour compound: at high concentration it reads as curry, diluted it reads as maple syrup, caramel or burnt sugar.

name: Diacetyl
fact: Butter's own smell, made by bacteria as a fermentation byproduct — Leuconostoc and its relatives producing it as they sour cream into cultured buttermilk.

name: Skatole
fact: 3-methylindole — pig manure at full strength, and part of why white pepper occasionally develops a faecal off-note when its retting husk sits in stagnant rather than running water.

name: Linalool
fact: Most of lavender's smell is this one molecule — chemists use lavender oil as the reference standard other linalool-scented things get compared to.

name: Limonene
fact: The major component of citrus peel oil, and most of what you smell the instant you zest an orange.

name: Methional
fact: Heat breaks the amino acid methionine down into this — the same Strecker reaction that gives fried potato its cooked-potato smell, wherever else methionine turns up hot.

name: Celeriac
fact: The same species as celery, Apium graveolens, bred toward the root instead of the stalk.

name: Agave
fact: A genus native to the arid Americas. Blue agave takes seven to fourteen years to mature.

name: Pulque
fact: Agave sap fermented by Zymomonas mobilis, not yeast — a milky drink the Aztecs called metl octli.

name: Tequila
fact: Blue agave hearts are baked to convert their fructans to sugar, fermented, then distilled twice by law.

name: Cognac
fact: Twice-distilled wine, mostly Ugni Blanc grapes, aged at least two years in French oak.

name: Cassia
fact: Cinnamomum cassia, a different tree from true cinnamon — sold as 'cinnamon' in most supermarket jars.

name: Hexanal
fact: An aldehyde smelling of freshly cut grass, released the instant a leaf or green fruit's tissue is damaged.

name: Vanillin
fact: The single molecule behind vanilla's scent — first sold in 1874, synthesized from clove oil, not vanilla.

name: Furaneol
fact: Strawberry furanone, also called pineapple ketone — fruity at low concentration, caramellic at high.

name: Cinnamaldehyde
fact: The oily compound that is, chemically, cinnamon's flavour and smell — straight out of the bark oil.

name: Citral
fact: The lemon smell itself, as a molecule — lemongrass oil runs 65 to 85 percent citral by weight.

name: Allicin
fact: Odourless alliin becomes this the instant a garlic cell wall breaks — the enzyme alliinase does it in seconds.

name: Octenol
fact: Mushroom alcohol, first isolated from crushed matsutake in the 1930s — the reason mushrooms smell like this.

name: Eucalyptol
fact: Also called 1,8-cineole — 70 to 90 percent of eucalyptus oil by weight, and present in rosemary's too.

name: Theobromine
fact: Chocolate's stimulant, not caffeine — mild in humans, far more dangerous to dogs, who clear it more slowly.

name: Galangal
fact: Ginger's own family and a rhizome too, but sharper and more resinous — camphor where ginger is warm.

name: Garlic Powder
fact: Garlic, dehydrated and ground fine — the same clove with the water gone.

name: Onion Powder
fact: Onion, dehydrated and ground fine — the same bulb with the water and the sting gone.

name: Garam Masala
fact: Northern India's best-known spice blend — 'garam' means warming, not spicy-hot.

name: Curry Powder
fact: A British colonial approximation — no South Asian region cooks from one fixed spice mix called 'curry powder'.

name: Five-Spice Powder
fact: Built to carry all five flavours Chinese cooking names — sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty — in one jar.

name: Berbere
fact: Ethiopia and Eritrea's base hot spice blend — the flavour underneath doro wat and most other stews.

name: Ras el Hanout
fact: Arabic for 'head of the shop' — once a merchant's own signature top-shelf mix, not one fixed recipe.

name: Herbes de Provence
fact: Sold pre-mixed since the 1970s — Provençal cooks once used these herbs individually, not blended.

name: Quatre Épices
fact: French for 'four spices' — a charcuterie seasoning built to warm pâtés and terrines without adding real heat.

name: Za'atar
fact: Both an Eastern Mediterranean herb and the tangy sesame-and-sumac mix named after it.

name: Harissa
fact: Tunisia's national chile paste, now spread across North African and French cooking.

name: Tabil
fact: Tunisian for 'seasoning' — once just ground coriander alone, now a fixed four-ingredient mix.

name: Chermoula
fact: A North African herb-and-spice marinade for fish, made fresh to order rather than jarred and stored.

name: Dukkah
fact: Egyptian for 'to pound' — nuts and seeds crushed together, eaten as a dip, not cooked into a dish.

name: Gomasio
fact: A Japanese table seasoning — just enough salt to season sesame without burying its toasted flavour.

name: Shichimi Togarashi
fact: Japanese 'seven-flavour chile' — a table shake-on built to layer heat, citrus, nuttiness and crunch at once.

name: Thai Curry Paste
fact: The pounded aromatic base under Thai curries — chiles, herbs and roots worked into a paste, not a dry powder.

name: Jerk Seasoning
fact: Jamaica's barbecue seasoning, named for the motion of piercing meat to work the spice in.

name: Seven Spices
fact: Lebanon's everyday warming blend — baharat, Arabic for 'spices', under a regional name.

name: Baharat
fact: Arabic simply for 'spices' — a warming, peppery blend that shifts country to country under the same name.

name: Hawaij
fact: A Yemenite Jewish spice blend stirred into soup; a second, sweeter version flavours coffee and cakes.

name: Advieh
fact: Persian for 'spices' — a rose-and-warm-spice blend, garam masala's distant cousin down the old spice routes.

name: Pickling Spice
fact: A whole-spice mix, never ground, so it can be lifted or strained back out of the brine once its work is done.

name: Fines Herbes
fact: Stirred in at the very end of cooking, unlike a dried bouquet garni — the point is fresh, fragile flavour.

name: Gingerbread Spice Mix
fact: Named for its loudest spice, though it is really a small family of warming spices working together.

name: Speculaas Spice
fact: The spice mix behind Dutch and Belgian speculaas cookies — a legacy of trade with the old Spice Islands.

name: Apple Pie Spice
fact: A mixture of sweet spices used to season American apple pie, in many household versions.

name: Pumpkin Pie Spice
fact: A branded product name before it was a category — now sold well beyond pumpkin pie, in lattes and cereal.

name: Poultry Seasoning
fact: An American spice-cabinet staple built specifically for turkey and chicken, not a general all-purpose blend.

name: Crawfish Boil Spices
fact: A whole-spice mix tied in a bag and simmered in the boiling water itself, not rubbed onto the shellfish.

name: Cajun Seasoning
fact: Louisiana's blackening-and-frying spice mix, built around cayenne heat rather than a dried-chile base.

name: Chesapeake Bay Seasoning
fact: A 1940s Baltimore blend that became the model for the world-famous, still-secret Old Bay Seasoning.

name: Adobo Seasoning
fact: Not the Filipino braising dish of the same name — a dry rub used across Latin American cooking.

name: Barbecue Seasoning Rub
fact: Rubbed onto meat before cooking, unlike a sauce — built to survive hours of smoke and heat.

name: Achiote Paste
fact: Yucatán's red seasoning paste, coloured by annatto seed, worked with citrus juice or vinegar, not oil.

name: Zhoug
fact: Yemen's fiery green condiment, now a fixture of Israeli cooking through its large Yemenite Jewish community.

name: Animism
fact: The belief that souls or spirits exist not only in humans but in animals, plants, rocks, and rivers — summed up by the Ainu saying that even a rock has a spirit.

name: Shamanism
fact: A practice in which a shaman enters trance — via drumming or, in some Siberian and Sami traditions, the fly agaric mushroom — to travel to and negotiate with the spirit world.

name: Ancestor Worship
fact: The belief that dead ancestors continue to exist and can influence, and be influenced by, the living, who owe them ongoing offerings and honor.

name: The Dreaming
fact: In Australian Aboriginal belief, the 'timeless time' of ongoing creation, in which ancestral beings shaped the land and left it charged with living spiritual power.

name: Human Sacrifice
fact: Ritual killing offered to the gods; Aztec priests cut the heart from a living victim, believing the sun needed a steady offering of human hearts and blood.

name: Ahura Mazda
fact: Zoroastrianism's supreme god, the 'Wise Lord' and sovereign creator of all good, worshipped through the sacred fire kept burning in every temple.

name: Angra Mainyu
fact: Zoroastrianism's destructive spirit, also called Ahriman, the eternal opponent of Ahura Mazda, who is said to have created the serpent-demon Aži Dahāka as an agent of chaos.

name: Zoroaster
fact: Persian prophet who reported a revelation of Ahura Mazda by a riverbank around age 30, composed the Gathas hymns, and founded Zoroastrianism.

name: Zoroastrianism
fact: One of the world's oldest monotheistic faiths, centered on the eternal struggle between the good creator Ahura Mazda and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu.

name: Laozi
fact: Legendary sage credited with the Daode Jing; tradition holds he rode an ox out of China and, at the western border, wrote his wisdom down for a guard before vanishing.

name: Dao
fact: The 'Way' of Daoist philosophy: an enigmatic, unseen process of transformation that underlies and sustains all reality.

name: Wu Wei
fact: Daoism's ideal of 'effortless action' — acting in such silent harmony with the dao that it may seem motionless, rather than striving against the current of things.

name: Daoism
fact: A Chinese religious philosophy founded on Laozi's Daode Jing, holding that the dao sustains and orders the universe and is best followed through wu wei, effortless action.

name: Mahavira
fact: Prince Vardhamana, who renounced his throne and family at 30 to live as a wandering ascetic; after 12 years of extreme austerity he attained enlightenment as Mahavira.

name: Ahimsa
fact: Jainism's vow of nonviolence, held to extend to the smallest organisms in water or air — why strict Jains strain their drinking water and watch where they walk.

name: Tirthankara
fact: A 'ford-builder' who shows others the way across the ocean of rebirth; Jains revere 24 per era, with Mahavira honored as the most recent of this cycle.

name: Jainism
fact: The most ascetic of India's major religions, shaped by Mahavira in the 6th century BCE around ahimsa — nonviolence toward all living things — as its highest duty.

name: Confucianism
fact: A Chinese ethical and religious tradition grown from Confucius's sayings, which his disciples collected and jointly edited into the Analects after his death.

name: Junzi
fact: Confucianism's ideal 'superior man,' who rules and lives by acting virtuously himself, on the belief that pure virtue draws others to follow by simple example.

name: Marduk
fact: Chief god of Babylon; he defeated the primordial sea-dragon Tiamat in battle, was crowned king of the gods, and fashioned the ordered world from her body.

name: Enûma Eliš
fact: Babylon's epic of creation, recorded on seven clay tablets, telling how Marduk defeated Tiamat and organized the cosmos — legitimizing Babylonian kingship.

name: Mummification
fact: Egyptian embalmers dried the body for 70 days in natron, a natural salt, before wrapping it in linen — a rite myth credits to the jackal-headed god Anubis, who first embalmed Osiris.

name: Book of the Dead
fact: A collection of funerary spells buried with wealthy Egyptians, meant to guide the deceased safely through the underworld and into the afterlife.

name: Shinto
fact: Japan's indigenous religion, venerating kami, the sacred spirits of nature, ancestors, and history, and tracing its roots to the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami.

name: Kami
fact: The sacred spirits Shinto venerates; the sun goddess Amaterasu, most revered of all kami, is enshrined at Ise and represented by the Sacred Mirror.

name: Torii
fact: The gateless gate marking a Shinto shrine's entrance, traditionally built of wood, symbolizing the transition from the ordinary world into sacred ground.

name: Ragnarok
fact: Norse mythology's apocalypse, in which Odin and Loki end up on opposing sides of a final battle between gods and giants that destroys the world before it rises again.

name: Valhalla
fact: Odin's hall for warriors slain in battle, supplied nightly with meat from the boar Sæhrímnir — eaten and whole again by morning — and mead from the goat Heiðrún.

name: Oracle
fact: The Pythia, Apollo's oracle at Delphi, entered a trance — possibly from gases seeping through the rock — to deliver the god's cryptic prophecies to those who sought her.

name: Lares
fact: Roman guardian spirits, often linked to the ancestral dead, honored at a shrine by the household hearth-fire and, in their civic role, at crossroads across the community.

name: Bhagavad-Gita
fact: A dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna set within the epic Mahabharata, probably the single most popular scripture in all of Hinduism.

name: Dharma
fact: Right living, or moral duty, which varies by role — a soldier's dharma differs from a farmer's — and which the Bhagavad-Gita's Krishna tells Arjuna he must perform even against his own feelings.

name: Karma
fact: The seed sown by every intentional deed, whose fruit — good or bad — ripens across lifetimes to turn the great wheel of rebirth.

name: Samsara
fact: The endless wheel of birth, death, and rebirth, kept turning by karma — a cycle broken only by moksha, liberation.

name: Atman
fact: One's innermost self, which the Upanishads locate within the heart and hold to be identical to Brahman, ultimate reality itself.

name: Brahman
fact: Ultimate, unchanging reality in Hindu philosophy, declared in the Upanishads' teaching 'tat tvam asi' — 'that thou art' — to be identical with the atman, the innermost self.

name: Moksha
fact: Liberation from the endless round of samsara, achieved by realizing that the atman, one's innermost self, is identical to Brahman, ultimate reality.

name: The Vedas
fact: Hinduism's four oldest and most authoritative scriptures — the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda — composed between roughly 1500 and 500 BCE.

name: The Upanishads
fact: The Vedas' philosophical final layer, moving from ritual toward the exploration of atman and Brahman; the word itself means 'sitting down near' a teacher.

name: Guru
fact: A teacher who passes on advanced spiritual knowledge to students — the word 'Upanishad' itself means 'sitting down near' the guru who imparts it.

name: Ashrama
fact: Hinduism's four life stages, taking a person from student, learning at a guru's side, to householder, to forest-dweller, and finally wandering ascetic.

name: Yoga
fact: A discipline combining physical postures with breath control to calm the mind until it can perceive the atman, the true self, and so attain liberation.

name: Puja
fact: Hindu ritual worship — the loving offering of light, flowers, water, or food before the image of a deity — open to any devotee, not only priests.

name: Bhakti
fact: Loving devotion to a personal god, which finds its most celebrated expression in the romantic devotion between Krishna and Radha.

name: Adi Shankara
fact: 8th-century Vedic philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on the Upanishads and Brahma Sutras, systematizing what became known as Advaita Vedanta.

name: Advaita Vedanta
fact: Adi Shankara's 'non-dual' school of Hindu philosophy, holding that Brahman alone is ultimately real, while the everyday world of separate, multiple things is not fully real.

name: Shakti
fact: Feminine divine power personified as the Great Goddess, taking forms across Hindu tradition from the gentle Parvati to the fierce Durga and Kali.

name: Moses
fact: As an infant, Moses was hidden among the reeds of the Nile River in a basket, according to the Torah's account of his birth; he grew up to lead the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt.

name: Abraham
fact: In Genesis, God promises the childless, desert-dwelling Abraham that his descendants will be as numerous as the stars in the sky; Jews, Christians, and Muslims all trace their religious ancestry back to him.

name: Jesus
fact: At the Last Supper, Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples and told them, 'Do this in remembrance of me' — the origin of the Christian Eucharist, or Holy Communion.

name: Muhammad
fact: Before his first revelation, Muhammad worked as a merchant leading camel caravans on the trade route to Syria for the wealthy widow Khadija, whom he later married.

name: Buddha
fact: Prince Siddhartha Gautama renounced his crown and sat beneath a fig tree, meditating until he reached enlightenment and became known as the Buddha, 'the Enlightened One.'

name: Guru Nanak
fact: A Hindu poet who debated with Hindu and Muslim holy men alike, Guru Nanak vanished into a river for three days and returned declaring, 'There is no Hindu, no Muslim.'

name: Zarathustra
fact: At about age 30, Zoroaster experienced a revelation of Ahura Mazda, the 'Wise Lord,' and described existence as an ongoing battle between truth and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu.

name: Thomas Henry Huxley
fact: Known as 'Darwin's Bulldog' for his fierce public defense of evolution, including a famous 1860 debate with Bishop Samuel Wilberforce, biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the word 'agnostic' in 1869.

name: Soul
fact: The words for 'spirit' in Latin (spiritus) and Greek (pneuma) both mean 'breath' or 'wind' — many traditions picture the soul as the breath that animates a body and departs at death.

name: Reincarnation
fact: The belief that after death, the nonmaterial essence of a person begins a new life in a new body — a central tenet of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, shaped by the karma accumulated in past lives.

name: Nirvana
fact: Nirvana literally means 'blowing out' or 'quenching' — early Buddhist texts pictured it as a flame going out once the fires of craving, hatred, and ignorance have burned themselves to nothing.

name: Torah
fact: The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally believed to have been revealed by God to Moses atop Mount Sinai.

name: Talmud
fact: Compiled by rabbis over centuries of debate on how to interpret and apply the Torah, the Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.

name: Tanakh
fact: An acronym for its three sections — Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings) — the Tanakh is the canon of the Hebrew Bible.

name: Quran
fact: Muslims believe the Quran's first verses were revealed to Muhammad by the angel Gabriel in the Cave of Hira, near Mecca, in 610 CE; revelations continued for 23 years.

name: Bible
fact: The Christian Bible unites the Hebrew scriptures as its Old Testament with a New Testament of gospels and letters recounting the life and teachings of Jesus.

name: Guru Granth Sahib
fact: Composed predominantly by six Sikh Gurus and compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, the Guru Granth Sahib was declared the Sikhs' eternal, living Guru by Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.

name: Trinity
fact: The Christian doctrine that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one being; legend credits Saint Patrick with using a three-leaved shamrock to explain it to the Irish.

name: Five Pillars
fact: The five obligatory acts of Islam: declaring the faith (Shahada), praying five times daily (Salat), giving to charity (Zakat), fasting during Ramadan (Sawm), and, if able, a pilgrimage to Mecca (Hajj).

name: Hinduism
fact: Hinduism has no single founder; many of its traditions hold that a single Supreme Reality, Brahman, is expressed through gods such as the Trimurti and taught in the ancient Vedas.

name: Buddhism
fact: Founded on the dharma the Buddha taught after his enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, Buddhism holds that suffering ends by following the Noble Eightfold Path.

name: Judaism
fact: The oldest of the Abrahamic religions, built on God's covenant with Abraham and on the Torah, the law revealed to Moses.

name: Christianity
fact: Centered on Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe to be the Son of God; God is understood as a Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

name: Islam
fact: Founded in 7th-century Arabia when Muhammad began receiving revelations later collected as the Quran, Islam teaches submission to the one God, Allah.

name: Taoism
fact: Traditionally traced to the sage Laozi, Taoism teaches that harmony comes from living according to the Tao ('the Way') and keeping yin and yang in balance.

name: Sikhism
fact: Founded by Guru Nanak in 15th-century Punjab, Sikhism's line of living Gurus ended in 1708, when Guru Gobind Singh named the Guru Granth Sahib itself as his eternal successor.

name: Atheism
fact: The absence of belief in gods; Charles Darwin's 1859 On the Origin of Species offered a natural explanation for life's diversity that many atheists point to as evidence a creator isn't needed.

name: Agnosticism
fact: The view that God's existence can never be proven or disproven; biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the term in 1869, from the Greek for 'not knowable.'

name: Yin and Yang
fact: Yin (dark, moist, cold, feminine — traditionally likened to moonlight) and yang (light, dry, warm, masculine — likened to fire and sunlight) are pictured as complementary halves that must stay in balance.

name: Om
fact: Considered the primordial sound of the universe, the sacred syllable Om (or Aum) is chanted across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism alike.

name: Mecca
fact: Islam's holiest city, in Saudi Arabia: birthplace of Muhammad and home to the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine built around the sacred Black Stone at the center of the Grand Mosque.

name: Synagogue
fact: A Jewish house of worship built around an ark that holds its Torah scrolls; full communal prayer traditionally requires a minyan, a quorum of at least ten adults.

name: Mosque
fact: An Islamic place of worship with a mihrab, a niche set into the wall to indicate the direction of Mecca, so that everyone can pray facing the same way.

name: Church
fact: Names both a building used for Christian worship and, more broadly, the entire community of Christian believers gathered around it.

name: Hindu Temple
fact: Most everyday Hindu worship happens at home shrines, but grand stone temples such as the Brihadisvara Temple, built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE, host puja, ritual devotional worship, on a monumental scale.

name: Rabbi
fact: A teacher and spiritual leader qualified to interpret Jewish law; the title comes from the Hebrew for 'my master,' and rabbis are the primary voices behind the Talmud's centuries of legal debate.

name: Cubeb
fact: Black pepper's own genus, picked unripe and dried whole with its stalk — the “tail” in tailed pepper.

name: Elecampane
fact: A tall Asteraceae with sunflower-like blooms, grown not for its flower but its bitter, camphor-scented root.

name: Licorice
fact: Glycyrrhiza glabra, a Fabaceae legume grown for its root — 50 times sweeter than sugar, and the source of glycyrrhizin.

name: Myrtle
fact: An evergreen Mediterranean shrub whose blue-black berries flavour the Sardinian liqueur Mirto.

name: Nigella
fact: Ranunculaceae — the same family as poisonous aconite — but nigella's black seed is a food-safe spice from Turkey to India.

name: Quassia
fact: Simaroubaceae bark named for Graman Quassi, the formerly enslaved Surinamese man credited with finding its medicinal use.

name: Safflower
fact: A drought-tolerant Asteraceae thistle bred for oil-rich seed and for petals that yield both a yellow and a red dye.

name: Sichuan Pepper
fact: Zanthoxylum's dried fruit husk — citrus and rue's own family, not pepper's — source of the tingling numbness sanshool.

name: Capers
fact: Capparis spinosa's flower buds, hand-picked each morning before they open and pickled in salt or vinegar.

name: Java Galangal
fact: Alpinia galanga, greater galangal — the same genus as lesser galangal but a far bigger plant, grown across tropical Java.

name: Asafoetida
fact: A Ferula gum-resin from Afghanistan and Iran, scored from the taproot and dried into a garlic-strong lump.

name: Grains of Paradise
fact: Aframomum melegueta — ginger's own family, the one cardamom belongs to — a pepper substitute from West African wetlands.

name: Carvone
fact: Caraway's own S-enantiomer smells of rye; the same molecule's mirror image, R-carvone, is spearmint.

name: Glycyrrhizin
fact: 50 times sweeter than sugar — and, in enough of it for long enough, the reason licorice root can raise blood pressure.

name: Sanshool
fact: Sichuan pepper's own tingle — closer to a mild electric buzz than to chili or black pepper's heat.

name: Carthamin
fact: Safflower's own alcohol-soluble red pigment, used as a natural rouge and lip colour since antiquity.

name: Cubeb Oil
fact: Steam-distilled from cubeb berries — a Victorian antiseptic sold specifically against gonorrhoea.

name: Black Seed Oil
fact: Cold-pressed nigella seed, sold today for its thymoquinone — still “under basic research,” not an established medicine.

name: Quassin
fact: Quassia bark's intensely bitter compound — flavoured bitters and beer for centuries, studied today as an insecticide.

name: Alantolactone
fact: Elecampane root's own sesquiterpene lactone, part of why herbalists still reach for it as an expectorant.

name: Monotheism
fact: Belief in a single, all-powerful God, as held by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

name: Polytheism
fact: Belief in and worship of multiple gods, each often linked to a different domain of life.

name: Religious Syncretism
fact: The blending of beliefs and practices from different religious traditions into a new, combined form.

name: Incarnation
fact: The idea that a deity can take on bodily, often human, form.

name: Messiah
fact: Hebrew for "anointed one"; a figure expected by Jewish tradition to deliver Israel.

name: Covenant
fact: In Judaism, the sacred agreement between God and Israel, given through Moses.

name: Ancestor Veneration
fact: Ritual honoring and offerings made to deceased forebears, believed to still watch over the living.

name: Filial Piety
fact: The Confucian virtue of respecting, obeying, and caring for one's parents and elders.

name: Asceticism
fact: A disciplined life of self-denial and renunciation practiced for spiritual purposes.

name: Pilgrimage
fact: A journey to a sacred place, undertaken for devotion, in nearly every major religion.

name: Mantra
fact: A sacred sound, word, or phrase repeated in prayer or meditation.

name: Incense
fact: Aromatic material burned as an offering or for ritual purification across many religions.

name: Cross
fact: An execution device in the Roman Empire that became Christianity's principal symbol.

name: Tomatillo
fact: A nightshade wrapped in its own papery lantern — the calyx husk it ripens inside. Aztec and Maya cooks used it before the tomato ever reached their kitchens.

name: Physalis
fact: A marble-sized orange berry sealed inside its own inflated paper husk — packaging good enough to keep the fruit fresh for over a month at room temperature.

name: Calamansi
fact: A kumquat-mandarin hybrid small enough to be mistaken for a lime. The Philippines alone exports up to 190,000 tonnes of its juice a year.

name: Yerba Mate
fact: A holly, not a tea plant. Its branches are dried over a wood fire, which is where mate's smoky note comes from, and its caffeine content sits between tea's and coffee's.

name: Bergamot
fact: Too bitter to eat — grown almost entirely for its peel oil, and a hundred bergamot oranges yield only about 85 grams of it. One Italian province supplies nearly all the world's.

name: Jasmine
fact: Blooms for one night only, releasing its scent for 12 to 20 hours before closing for good — pickers take only unopened white buds, since green ones never develop the fragrance.

name: Plantain
fact: A sterile triploid hybrid of two wild bananas, bred for starch instead of sugar, which is why it's always cooked and never eaten raw.

name: Black Cardamom
fact: Dried over an open flame instead of in the sun, which is why it tastes of campfire smoke instead of green cardamom's mint and lemon. Nepal grows more of it than anywhere else.

name: Butternut Squash
fact: A 1944 invention, not an old heirloom — Massachusetts grower Charles Leggett crossed gooseneck and Hubbard squash to make it, and botanically it's classed as a berry.

name: Nasturtium
fact: Every part above ground is edible, peppery like watercress — and its round leaves are so water-repellent that rain beads up and rolls clean off.

name: Perilla
fact: Called shiso in Japan, deulkkae in Korea and zisu in China — a mint-family leaf that's also a livestock hazard: cattle that graze on it can develop fatal respiratory distress.

name: Wormwood
fact: Chernobyl is named for it — Old Slavic for 'black grass' — and its bitter compound, thujone, has never actually been proven to be what made 19th-century absinthe dangerous.

name: Doenjang
fact: Korea's own miso, but not built on koji — its meju bricks grow a wild mould in open air for weeks before they ever touch brine.

name: Gochujang
fact: Korea's chilli didn't arrive until the 1500s, carried in by Portuguese traders — yet the fermented pepper paste it made possible has its own centuries-old home town: Sunchang.

name: Geraniol
fact: Bees paint it on flowers to mark them already-visited, and dab it at the hive entrance so stragglers can find their way home.

name: Beta-Ionone
fact: The scent of violets, made by snapping beta-carotene in half. Roughly a quarter of people carry a gene variant that makes them smell vinegar instead of flowers.

name: Ethyl Hexanoate
fact: The pineapple-and-apple-peel note inside a wedge of blue cheese — the same ester that turns up in beer and port, part of why cheese pairs so well with both.

name: Dimethyl Trisulfide
fact: Detectable at one part per trillion, foul enough to draw blowflies to a corpse — and the same molecule that gives black truffle and blue cheese part of their pungent kick.

name: Sufism
fact: Islam's mystical tradition, seeking union with God through practices like dhikr and ecstatic whirling dance.

name: Ahmadiyya
fact: Islamic reform movement founded 1889 in Punjab by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, who claimed to be the Mahdi.

name: Shia Islam
fact: Second-largest Islamic branch, holding that Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, was his rightful successor.

name: Sunni Islam
fact: Islam's largest branch (85-90% of Muslims), following Muhammad's sunnah and consensus-chosen caliphs.

name: Sharia
fact: Islamic legal and ethical code from the Qur'an and Sunnah; its name literally means 'path to water.'

name: Jihad
fact: Islamic duty to strive in God's way -- the inner 'greater jihad' against one's own vices, or armed struggle.

name: Wahhabism
fact: Conservative Sunni revivalist movement founded in 18th-century Najd, allied since 1744 with the Saudi dynasty.

name: Salafism
fact: Sunni revivalist movement (from 'salaf,' predecessors) urging return to early Islam's first generations.

name: Nation of Islam
fact: African American religious-political movement founded in Detroit, 1930, by Wallace Fard Muhammad.

name: Druze
fact: Small esoteric faith split from Ismaili Islam near Cairo, c.1017 CE, teaching reincarnation of the soul.

name: Baha'i Faith
fact: Monotheistic faith founded by Baha'u'llah in 19th-century Persia, teaching unity of God and humanity.

name: Rastafari
fact: Afro-Jamaican movement from the 1930s that reveres Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie I as a divine figure.

name: Santeria
fact: Syncretic Cuban religion, 19th century, blending Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saint veneration.

name: Haitian Vodou
fact: Syncretic Haitian religion blending West and Central African traditions with Catholicism; its spirits are lwa.

name: Cargo Cult
fact: 20th-century Pacific Islander movements believing Western manufactured goods were spirit-sent 'cargo.'

name: Scientology
fact: Belief system L. Ron Hubbard developed from his 1950 book Dianetics, centered on 'auditing' sessions.

name: Unification Church
fact: New religious movement founded 1954 in Seoul by Sun Myung Moon, known for mass wedding 'Blessing' rites.

name: Wicca
fact: Modern Pagan religion popularized in 1950s England by Gerald Gardner, venerating a Horned God and Goddess.

name: Unitarian Universalism
fact: Creedless US faith formed in 1961 from the Unitarian and Universalist churches; symbol is the flaming chalice.

name: Hare Krishna Movement
fact: ISKCON, founded in New York, 1966, by Prabhupada; devotees chant the Hare Krishna mantra in saffron robes.

name: Falun Dafa
fact: Chinese spiritual practice founded 1992 by Li Hongzhi, blending qigong with moral teaching; banned since 1999.

name: Tenrikyo
fact: Japanese new religion founded 1838 by Nakayama Miki, who recorded revelations in the sacred Ofudesaki.

name: Cao Dai
fact: Syncretic Vietnamese religion founded 1926, uniting Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian, and Catholic elements.

name: Jehovah's Witnesses
fact: Christian movement from 1870s Pittsburgh, known for door-to-door evangelism and refusing blood transfusions.

name: Mormonism
fact: Faith founded 1830 in New York by Joseph Smith, based on the Book of Mormon translated from golden plates.

name: Quakers
fact: Religious Society of Friends, founded mid-1600s England by George Fox, worshipping largely in silence.

name: Amish
fact: Traditionalist Christians who split from the Mennonites in 1693, rejecting modern technology.

name: Mennonites
fact: Anabaptist Christians named for reformer Menno Simons, baptizing only adult believers, not infants.

name: Shakers
fact: Celibate US religious sect founded by Ann Lee, c.1747, famed for plain furniture and ecstatic worship.

name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
fact: Christian denomination established 1863 in Michigan, observing Saturday Sabbath and vegetarian diet.

name: Pentecostalism
fact: Christian movement from the 1906 Azusa Street Revival, emphasizing speaking in tongues.

name: Christian Science
fact: Church founded 1879 in Boston by Mary Baker Eddy, relying on prayer rather than medicine for healing.

name: The Salvation Army
fact: Christian charity founded 1865 in London by William Booth, with military ranks and Christmas kettles.

name: Anglicanism
fact: Church of England, founded 1534 when Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy broke from Rome.

name: Lutheranism
fact: Protestant tradition begun 1517 by Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against indulgences.

name: Presbyterianism
fact: Reformed Protestant tradition from Calvin and Knox, governed by elected elders, or 'presbyters.'

name: Methodism
fact: Revival movement within Anglicanism founded by John Wesley, whose 1738 conversion sparked its growth.

name: Baptists
fact: Protestant tradition from 1609, practicing believer's baptism by full immersion, not infant baptism.

name: Reform Judaism
fact: Modernizing Jewish movement from early 19th-century Germany, emphasizing ethics over ritual observance.

name: Orthodox Judaism
fact: Traditionalist Jewish movement that crystallized in the 1818-21 Hamburg Temple dispute.

name: Hasidic Judaism
fact: Mystical Jewish revival founded c.1740 by the Baal Shem Tov, emphasizing joyful, ecstatic devotion.

name: Conservative Judaism
fact: US Jewish movement centered on the Jewish Theological Seminary, a middle path between Reform and Orthodox.

name: Kabbalah
fact: Jewish mysticism whose text, the Zohar, appeared in 13th-century Spain, describing ten divine sefirot.

name: Vaishnavism
fact: Largest Hindu devotional tradition, revering Vishnu and his avatars Rama and Krishna as supreme.

name: Shaivism
fact: Major Hindu tradition centered on Shiva as supreme deity, marked by sacred ash and the lingam symbol.

name: Shaktism
fact: Hindu tradition worshipping the Goddess, Devi or Shakti, as ultimate reality, since Vedic times.

name: Arya Samaj
fact: Hindu reform movement founded 1875 in Bombay by Swami Dayananda Saraswati, opposing idol worship.

name: Transcendental Meditation
fact: Mantra-based meditation brought West in 1955 by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, popularized by the Beatles.

name: Theravada Buddhism
fact: Oldest surviving Buddhist school, based on the Pali Canon, dominant in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

name: Mahayana Buddhism
fact: Buddhist tradition emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal, dominant in China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan.

name: Zen Buddhism
fact: Meditation-focused Buddhist school, from China's Chan, brought to Japan; centers on seated zazen.

name: Tibetan Buddhism
fact: Buddhism of the Tibetan Empire, 7th-9th centuries, led by reincarnating lamas like the Dalai Lama.

name: Pure Land Buddhism
fact: Chinese Buddhist tradition devoted to Amitabha Buddha, whose Pure Land paradise is reached by faith.

name: Nichiren Buddhism
fact: Japanese Buddhist school founded by the 13th-century monk Nichiren, centered on the Lotus Sutra.

name: Soka Gakkai
fact: Lay Buddhist movement founded 1930 in Japan by educators Makiguchi and Toda, rooted in Nichiren Buddhism.

name: Cuneiform
fact: Sumerian wedge-shaped script pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus, from Uruk around 3300 BCE.

discovered.note: First unequivocal written documents appear at Uruk in Sumer.

name: Code of Hammurabi
fact: Hammurabi's laws, cut in cuneiform onto a 7.5-foot basalt stele -- 'an eye for an eye' among ~300 clauses.

discovered.note: Composed late in Hammurabi's reign over Babylon.

name: Indus Valley Civilization
fact: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro: standardized fired-brick cities sharing one system of weights, with no found king.

discovered.note: Start of the civilization's mature, urbanized phase.

name: Oracle Bone
fact: Shang diviners cracked heated turtle shells and ox bones, then carved the question beside the crack.

discovered.note: Late Shang divination texts from Yinxu, near modern Anyang.

name: Shang Dynasty
fact: China's earliest dynasty confirmed by its own writing, casting bronze vessels for ritual, not daily use.

discovered.note: Traditional founding date; modern estimates run from the 16th to 11th century BCE.

name: Minoan Civilization
fact: Bronze Age Crete: masted ships carried trade to Egypt and Syria; palace at Knossos anchored the Aegean.

discovered.note: Early Minoan II: Cretan ships begin sailing beyond the Aegean.

name: Mycenaean Greece
fact: Mainland Greeks who took Minoan Crete and adapted Linear A into Linear B, the earliest written Greek.

discovered.note: A Mycenaean elite takes over the palace of Knossos on Crete.

name: Bronze Age Collapse
fact: Mycenaean Greece, the Hittite Empire, and Ugarit fell within decades, as iron began spreading in.

discovered.note: Widespread systems collapse across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East.

name: Phoenician Alphabet
fact: Phoenician traders' phonetic script spread round the Mediterranean, ancestor of Greek, then Latin.

discovered.note: Conventional date for the script's emergence; earliest confirmed inscriptions are 10th century BCE.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
fact: Ruled from Nineveh in cuneiform; Ashurbanipal's library held 30,000+ tablets, including Gilgamesh.

discovered.note: Empire begins with the accession of Adad-nirari II.

name: Cyrus the Great
fact: Founder of Persia's Achaemenid Empire; took Babylon in 539 BCE nearly without a fight, freeing its exiles.

discovered.note: Cyrus enters Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

name: Battle of Marathon
fact: Outnumbered roughly 2 to 1, Athenian hoplites broke Darius I's invading Persians at Marathon.

discovered.note: Athens and Plataea defeat the Persian invasion force.

name: Alexander the Great
fact: Broke Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, conquering the Persian Empire Cyrus founded two centuries before.

discovered.note: Achaemenid rule ends as Alexander completes his conquest of Persia.

name: Qin Shi Huang
fact: China's First Emperor, buried near Xi'an behind thousands of individually crafted terracotta soldiers.

discovered.note: Qin conquers the last rival state, unifying China.

name: Ashoka
fact: Maurya emperor who, remorseful after conquering Kalinga, carved Buddhist edicts onto rocks and pillars.

discovered.note: The Kalinga War, in the eighth year of Ashoka's reign, precedes his edicts.

name: Carthage
fact: Phoenician colony on the North African coast, its name meaning 'new city' -- in legend founded by Dido.

discovered.note: Archaeology dates Carthage's earliest urban settlement to the 7th century BCE.

name: Hannibal
fact: Carthaginian general who led 38,000 troops and 38 war elephants across the Alps; almost none survived.

discovered.note: Hannibal crosses the Alps, opening the Second Punic War.

name: Julius Caesar
fact: Led his legion across the Rubicon in defiance of the Senate, igniting Rome's civil war.

discovered.note: Caesar crosses the Rubicon River.

name: Cleopatra
fact: Last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy after his empire split apart.

discovered.note: Cleopatra VII becomes queen of Ptolemaic Egypt.

name: Augustus
fact: Caesar's heir Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium and became Rome's first emperor.

discovered.note: The Senate grants Octavian the title Augustus.

name: Silk Road
fact: Camel caravans carried China's silk to Rome, where the Senate banned it in vain as decadent.

discovered.note: Han dynasty embassies follow envoy Zhang Qian's reports on Central Asia.

name: Kingdom of Kush
fact: Nubian kingdom whose King Piye conquered Egypt to found its 25th Dynasty; later capital Meroe smelted iron.

discovered.note: Piye seizes control of Lower Egypt, founding Kush's 25th Dynasty.

name: Mahatma Gandhi
fact: Led India's independence movement through nonviolent civil disobedience, or satyagraha.

name: Four Noble Truths
fact: The Buddha's first sermon: suffering exists, it has a cause, it can end, and a path leads there.

name: Noble Eightfold Path
fact: Eight practices of wisdom, ethics, and discipline — Buddhism's Fourth Noble Truth.

name: Middle Way
fact: The Buddha's path of moderation between luxury and extreme self-denial.

name: Bodhisattva
fact: In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who delays their own nirvana to help all others reach it.

name: Dalai Lama
fact: Leader of Tibetan Buddhism's Gelug school, held to be compassion reborn in human form.

name: Ashoka
fact: Mauryan emperor whose stone-carved edicts promoted Buddhist nonviolence across ancient India.

name: Ten Commandments
fact: The core laws of the covenant at Sinai, inscribed on stone tablets given to Moses.

name: Diaspora
fact: Jewish communities dispersed across the world after repeated exile from their homeland.

name: Maimonides
fact: 12th-century philosopher and physician who argued God's oneness allows no parts or attributes.

name: Nicene Creed
fact: The Christian statement of belief adopted at Nicaea in 325 CE and expanded in 381 CE.

name: Eucharist
fact: Christian ritual reenacting Jesus's Last Supper, sharing bread and wine as his body and blood.

name: Baptism
fact: Christian rite of initiation through ritual washing with water, following Jesus's own baptism.

name: Monasticism
fact: Christians withdrawing from ordinary life to devote themselves to prayer, discipline, and study.

name: Protestant Reformation
fact: The 16th-century split from the Catholic Church sparked by Luther's protest against indulgences.

name: Chain
fact: Iron rings forged and closed while hot, then linked before they cool. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

name: Key
fact: A sliver of metal cut to match one lock's internal wards, so only its owner — not a thief — can open a door.

name: Prometheus
fact: Titan who fashioned humanity from clay and stole fire from the gods; chained to a rock, an eagle ate his regrowing liver daily.

name: Epimetheus
fact: Prometheus's foolish brother — his name means "afterthought" — who ignored every warning and married Pandora anyway.

name: Pandora
fact: The first woman, molded from clay by Hephaestus and given every grace by the gods, along with a jar she could not resist opening.

name: Pandora's Jar
fact: The jar Pandora opened despite every warning, loosing every evil into the world — only Hope stayed trapped inside.

name: Atlas
fact: Titan condemned by Zeus to hold up the heavens forever, punishment for leading the Titans against the Olympians.

name: Deucalion
fact: Prometheus's son, who built a chest to survive Zeus's flood, then repopulated the earth by throwing stones over his shoulder.

name: Pyrrha
fact: Deucalion's wife and fellow flood survivor, whose stones thrown over her shoulder became the first women.

name: Daedalus
fact: Athenian inventor who built Crete's Labyrinth, then fashioned feather-and-wax wings to fly himself and his son off the island.

name: Icarus
fact: Daedalus's son, who ignored his father's warning, flew too near the sun on wax wings, and fell into the sea now named for him.

name: Phaethon
fact: Son of the sun god Helios, who begged to drive his father's chariot for a day and was struck from the sky by Zeus to save the earth.

name: Labyrinth
fact: The maze Daedalus built on Crete at King Minos's order, its passages winding so nothing inside could ever find its way out.

name: Minotaur
fact: Half-man, half-bull son of Queen Pasiphaë and a bull sent by Poseidon, imprisoned by King Minos inside the Labyrinth.

name: Theseus
fact: Athenian prince who volunteered as tribute to Crete and killed the Minotaur, escaping the Labyrinth with Ariadne's thread.

name: Ariadne
fact: Cretan princess whose ball of thread saved Theseus from the Labyrinth; abandoned on Naxos, she married the god Dionysus instead.

name: Perseus
fact: Son of Zeus, conceived as a shower of gold, who beheaded the Gorgon Medusa using a mirrored shield to avoid her petrifying gaze.

name: Medusa
fact: The one mortal Gorgon, her hair living snakes and her gaze turning onlookers to stone, until Perseus struck off her head.

name: Pegasus
fact: The winged horse that sprang fully grown from Medusa's neck the instant Perseus beheaded her.

name: Andromeda
fact: Aethiopian princess chained to a sea cliff as a monster's sacrifice for her mother's boast, until Perseus swept down to save her.

name: Golden Fleece
fact: The fleece of a winged golden ram, hung in a sacred Colchian grove and watched over by a dragon that never slept.

name: Jason
fact: Rightful heir to Iolcos, who sailed the Argo to Colchis and won the Golden Fleece — only with the sorceress Medea's help.

name: Medea
fact: Colchian sorceress whose narcotic herbs lulled the Golden Fleece's dragon to sleep; Jason's later betrayal turned her fury lethal.

name: Sphinx (Greek)
fact: Thebes's riddling monster — a woman's head, a lion's body, an eagle's wings — that strangled every traveler who answered wrong.

name: Oedipus
fact: Theban king who fulfilled a prophecy of patricide and incest without knowing it, after answering the Sphinx's riddle about man.

name: Orpheus
fact: Greek mythology's greatest musician, whose lyre-song nearly won his dead wife Eurydice back from the underworld.

name: Eurydice
fact: Orpheus's bride, killed by a snakebite and lost forever when he glanced back at her one step before reaching daylight.

name: Midas
fact: Phrygian king granted the golden touch by Dionysus — a blessing that turned his food, wine, and embrace into a curse.

name: Echo
fact: Nymph cursed by Hera to only repeat others' last words, punishment for distracting the goddess while Zeus roamed unseen.

name: Narcissus
fact: Beautiful youth who spurned the nymph Echo's love, then wasted away staring at his own reflection in a woodland pool.

name: Arachne
fact: Lydian weaver so skilled she challenged Athena herself; struck down for it, she was reborn as the world's first spider.

name: Atlantis
fact: Plato's fictional island empire, "larger than Libya and Asia," swallowed by the sea in a single day and night for its arrogance.

name: Psyche
fact: Mortal princess so beautiful people worshipped her over Venus; her secret husband was Cupid, and her trials led her to godhood.

name: Janus
fact: Roman god of doorways and beginnings, shown with two faces looking opposite ways at once — no Greek god has ever matched him.

name: Vesta
fact: Roman virgin goddess of the hearth; her eternal flame, tended by the Vestal Virgins in the Forum, was never allowed to go out.

name: Hestia
fact: Eldest child of Kronos, first swallowed and last disgorged; Greek goddess of the hearth fire at the center of every home.

name: Romulus
fact: Twin son of Mars, suckled by a she-wolf after being left to die as an infant; he founded Rome on the Palatine Hill in 753 BCE.

name: Remus
fact: Romulus's twin, also raised by the she-wolf; killed after mocking the walls of Rome's first, unfinished city.

name: Aeneas
fact: Trojan prince, son of the goddess Venus, who carried his father from burning Troy and became — in Virgil's telling — Rome's ancestor.

name: Numa Pompilius
fact: Sabine second king of Rome, who met nightly with the nymph Egeria and founded the Vestal cult, the priesthoods, and the calendar.

name: Cybele
fact: Anatolian "Great Mother" goddess, worshipped in Phrygia since the Bronze Age, brought to Rome in 204 BCE as a black meteoric stone.

name: Attis
fact: Cybele's devoted companion, who castrated himself beneath a pine tree in a fit of grief-madness and was reborn each spring.

name: Mithras
fact: Center of a secretive Roman soldiers' cult, worshipped underground for slaying the cosmic bull whose blood renewed the world.

name: Pygmalion
fact: Cypriot sculptor who fell in love with his own ivory statue; Venus answered his prayer by bringing her to life as Galatea.

name: Sibyl of Cumae
fact: Apollo's ancient prophetess, granted a lifespan measured in grains of dust but not eternal youth; she guided Aeneas through the Underworld.

name: Medina
fact: Yathrib's feuding tribes invited Muhammad to mediate in 622; his migration there began the Islamic calendar.

discovered.note: Muhammad's hijra (migration) from Mecca starts year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

name: Umayyad Caliphate
fact: Founded at Damascus in 661 by Mu'awiyah after the civil war that followed Caliph Ali's assassination.

discovered.note: Mu'awiyah becomes caliph after the First Fitna, founding the Umayyad dynasty at Damascus.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
fact: Overthrew the Umayyads in the 750 revolution, claiming descent from Muhammad's uncle Abbas.

discovered.note: The Abbasid Revolution, led by Abu Muslim from Khurasan, topples the Umayyad dynasty.

name: Baghdad
fact: Founded on the Tigris in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur; its House of Wisdom made it a center of learning.

discovered.note: Caliph al-Mansur commissions Baghdad's construction as the new Abbasid capital.

name: Seljuk Turks
fact: Turkic sultan Tugrul Beg took Baghdad in 1055, reducing the Abbasid caliph to a figurehead.

discovered.note: Tugrul Beg enters Baghdad and becomes the caliph's real power, styling himself sultan.

name: Byzantine Empire
fact: The eastern Roman Empire that outlived Rome; in 552 its monks broke China's monopoly on silk.

discovered.note: Monks smuggle silkworm eggs out of Central Asia, letting Byzantium found its own silk industry.

name: Crusades
fact: Launched in 1095 after Byzantine Emperor Alexius I begged Pope Urban II for help against the Seljuks.

discovered.note: Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont.

name: Cannon
fact: Cast in bronze in China by the 13th century; the 1298 Xanadu Gun is the earliest known survivor.

discovered.note: The Xanadu Gun, the earliest confirmed surviving cannon, is cast in Yuan China.

name: Ottoman Empire
fact: Mehmed II's cannons breached Constantinople's walls in 1453, ending Byzantium.

discovered.note: Sultan Mehmed II's forces storm Constantinople after a 53-day siege.

name: Genghis Khan
fact: Born Temüjin; united the Mongol clans at a 1206 assembly and took the title Genghis Khan.

discovered.note: Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai on the Onon River.

name: Mongol Empire
fact: Genghis Khan's conquests unified Central Asia, and the Pax Mongolica reopened the Silk Road.

discovered.note: Genghis Khan's unification of the Mongol clans launches the conquests that build the empire.

name: Black Death
fact: Mongol siege of Genoese Caffa in 1346 let plague reach ships that carried it to Sicily by 1347.

discovered.note: Plague reaches Crimea during the Mongol siege of the Genoese trading post of Caffa.

name: Kublai Khan
fact: Genghis Khan's grandson; completed the conquest of Song China and founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271.

discovered.note: Kublai Khan establishes the Yuan dynasty, ruling China as a Mongol emperor.

name: Yuan Dynasty
fact: Kublai Khan's Mongol dynasty in China, which issued jiaochao — an early nationwide paper currency.

discovered.note: Kublai Khan formally establishes the Yuan dynasty.

name: Ming Dynasty
fact: Peasant rebel Zhu Yuanzhang overthrew the Yuan in 1368, rising through the Red Turban Rebellion.

discovered.note: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims himself the Hongwu Emperor, founding the Ming dynasty.

name: Forbidden City
fact: Built 1406-1420 by the Ming Yongle Emperor from precious zhennan timber and specially baked brick.

discovered.note: Construction of the Yongle Emperor's new Beijing palace complex is completed.

name: Zheng He
fact: Ming eunuch admiral sent on seven treasure-fleet voyages, reaching East Africa by 1433.

discovered.note: Zheng He departs Suzhou on the first of his seven treasure voyages.

name: Qing Dynasty
fact: Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to Manchu forces in 1644, founding the Qing.

discovered.note: Manchu forces take Beijing through the Shanhai Pass, founding the Qing dynasty.

name: Samurai
fact: Japan's warrior class, originally mounted horse-archers from wealthy landholding families.

name: Katana
fact: Forged by folding and differentially tempering steel; the Tokugawa made it the samurai's badge.

name: Kamakura Shogunate
fact: Minamoto Yoritomo's naval win at Dan-no-ura in 1185 led to Japan's first military government in 1192.

discovered.note: Minamoto no Yoritomo is appointed shogun, founding the Kamakura shogunate.

name: Delhi Sultanate
fact: Founded in 1206 by the former slave Qutb-ud-din Aibak after Muhammad of Ghor's conquest of North India.

discovered.note: Qutb-ud-din Aibak becomes the first Sultan of Delhi after Muhammad of Ghor's death.

name: Tamerlane
fact: Styling himself Genghis Khan's heir, he built a Central Asian empire and sacked Delhi in 1398.

discovered.note: Timur's forces capture and sack Delhi, devastating the Sultanate.

name: Mughal Empire
fact: Babur, descended from Tamerlane and Genghis Khan, used cannon to smash the Delhi Sultanate in 1526.

discovered.note: Babur defeats the Lodi sultan at the First Battle of Panipat, founding the Mughal Empire.

name: Khmer Empire
fact: Founded by Jayavarman II in 802; its rice wealth came from a hydraulic network off the Tonlé Sap.

discovered.note: Jayavarman II's consecration ritual on Mount Mahendraparvata marks the empire's founding.

name: Angkor Wat
fact: Built 1122-1150 under Suryavarman II, its towers designed to represent Mount Meru, home of the gods.

discovered.note: Construction of Suryavarman II's temple-mountain at Angkor is completed.

name: Mali Empire
fact: Sundiata Keita founded it after the 1235 Battle of Kirina, taxing salt and gold across West Africa.

discovered.note: Sundiata Keita's victory at the Battle of Kirina founds the Mali Empire.

name: Mansa Musa
fact: His 1324-25 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly gave away enough gold to depress its price in Cairo for years.

discovered.note: Mansa Musa departs Mali on his roughly 2,700-mile pilgrimage to Mecca.

name: Aztec Empire
fact: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, building an empire on chinampa maize farming and obsidian arms.

discovered.note: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on a lake island, per legend where an eagle perched on a cactus.

name: Tenochtitlan
fact: The Aztec capital, built on a Lake Texcoco island and linked to the mainland by removable causeways.

discovered.note: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on its island site in Lake Texcoco.

name: Inca Empire
fact: Centered on Cuzco high in the Andes; expanded explosively from 1438 under the ruler Pachacuti.

discovered.note: Pachacuti becomes Sapa Inca and begins the empire's rapid expansion.

name: Machu Picchu
fact: A royal estate built for Pachacuti around 1450 on a mountain ridge, abandoned near the Spanish conquest.

discovered.note: Pachacuti orders the mountain estate built after his conquest of the Urubamba valley.

name: Hernán Cortés
fact: Landed in 1519 with 500 men, 13 horses, and Tlaxcalan allies; took Tenochtitlan by siege in 1521.

discovered.note: Cortés completes the siege and capture of Tenochtitlan, ending the Aztec Empire.

name: Francisco Pizarro
fact: Captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532; had him executed after a gold ransom in 1533.

discovered.note: Atahualpa is executed after his ransom is paid, and Pizarro's forces take Cuzco.

name: Smallpox Epidemic
fact: Arrived with Spanish forces in 1520 and killed thousands in Tenochtitlan, crippling Aztec resistance.

discovered.note: Smallpox, introduced by an infected member of a Spanish expedition, sweeps Tenochtitlan.

name: Martin Luther
fact: Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor who protested indulgence sales in his 1517 95 Theses.

discovered.note: Luther's 95 Theses protest the Church's sale of indulgences.

name: Hundred Years' War
fact: Fought 1337-1453 over the French throne; cannon debuted at Crécy and decided it at Castillon.

discovered.note: Edward III's claim to the French throne triggers open war.

name: Joan of Arc
fact: Broke the siege of Orléans in 1429; captured and burned at the stake as a heretic in 1431.

discovered.note: Joan of Arc's arrival helps break the English siege of Orléans.

name: Sumer
fact: City-states between the Tigris and Euphrates that gave the world its first cities, from 3000 BCE.

discovered.note: Uruk and the other Sumerian city-states become the world's first cities in southern Mesopotamia.

name: Akkadian Empire
fact: Sargon's conquest of Sumer around 2334 BCE built history's first empire.

discovered.note: Sargon of Akkad conquers Sumer's city-states, founding history's first empire.

name: Hittites
fact: Anatolian kingdom that fought Egypt to a standstill, then sealed history's earliest surviving treaty.

discovered.note: Hittites and Egyptians seal the earliest peace treaty to survive, after the Battle of Kadesh.

name: Minoan Crete
fact: Crete's sea-trading palace culture, famous for the bull-leaping frescoes of Knossos.

discovered.note: Minoan palace culture flourishes on Crete, centred on Knossos.

name: Mycenaeans
fact: Took Knossos from the Minoans and turned their script into the first written Greek.

discovered.note: Mycenaean Greeks take control of Knossos and adapt Linear A into Linear B.

name: Mohenjo-daro
fact: The Great Bath: a bitumen-sealed public water tank, among the oldest known in the world.

discovered.note: Mohenjo-daro is built as one of the Indus Valley's great planned cities.

name: Olmecs
fact: Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization, famous for colossal carved basalt heads.

discovered.note: The Olmecs, Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization, flourish on the Gulf coast.

name: Chavín Culture
fact: Spread a shared Andean religion of fanged jaguar gods, with no armies at all.

discovered.note: The temple at Chavín de Huántar becomes a pan-Andean religious centre.

name: Achaemenid Empire
fact: Cyrus's conquests built the largest empire the world had yet seen.

discovered.note: Cyrus the Great captures Babylon, founding the largest empire the world had yet seen.

name: Persepolis
fact: Darius's ceremonial capital, its Apadana built to host thousands -- burned by Alexander.

discovered.note: Darius I founds Persepolis as the Achaemenid Empire's ceremonial capital.

name: Hellenistic Culture
fact: Alexander's generals split his empire into rival Greek-ruled kingdoms.

discovered.note: Alexander's generals divide his empire into rival Hellenistic kingdoms.

name: Roman Republic
fact: Rome expelled its kings in 509 BCE and wrote its first laws onto bronze.

discovered.note: Rome expels its last king, Tarquinius Superbus, and becomes a republic.

name: Punic Wars
fact: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants and nearly destroyed Rome.

discovered.note: Hannibal crosses the Alps with war elephants, opening the Second Punic War.

name: Fall of Rome
fact: Huns pushed the Goths into Rome, who sacked it -- ending 500 years of empire.

discovered.note: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, ending the Western Roman Empire.

name: Celts
fact: Iron Age Europe's ironworking, chariot-fighting, hillfort-building warrior culture.

discovered.note: The iron-rich, chariot-fighting La Tène culture spreads across Iron Age Europe.

name: Scythians
fact: Steppe archers who buried their dead in gold-heavy kurgan mounds.

discovered.note: Scythian nomads become established on the Pontic-Caspian steppe.

name: Huns
fact: Broke the steppe empire that had displaced the Scythians, then turned on Rome.

discovered.note: Huns crush the Alans and Sarmatians on the Pontic steppe, setting off Rome's crisis.

name: Mauryan Empire
fact: Chandragupta traded 500 war elephants to Alexander's former general for land.

discovered.note: Chandragupta Maurya founds India's first empire.

name: Gupta Empire
fact: Chandragupta I's dynasty, ruling from the old Mauryan capital of Pataliputra.

discovered.note: Chandragupta I builds the Gupta dynasty into an empire from Pataliputra.

name: Terracotta Army
fact: 8,000 unique clay soldiers guarding the First Emperor's tomb, found by well-diggers.

discovered.note: Qin Shi Huang is buried with an underground army of thousands of terracotta soldiers.

name: Han Dynasty
fact: Wudi's campaigns opened the Silk Road, carrying Chinese silk as far as Rome.

discovered.note: Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty after Qin's collapse.

name: Teotihuacan
fact: The Americas' largest ancient city, built on a monopoly of obsidian trade.

discovered.note: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun is completed.

name: Zapotec Civilization
fact: Built Monte Albán on neutral mountaintop ground between three rival valleys.

discovered.note: The Zapotecs found Monte Albán on a mountaintop above Oaxaca's three valleys.

name: Maya Civilization
fact: City-states like Tikal, built on maize, with kings enthroned on jaguar pelts.

discovered.note: The Classic period of Maya civilization begins, with city-states like Tikal.

name: Athenian Democracy
fact: Cleisthenes's Council of 500, and a vote of exile scratched onto broken pottery.

discovered.note: Cleisthenes's reforms found Athenian democracy.

name: Sparta
fact: Twin kings and a helot-farmed economy freed Spartan boys for lifelong war training.

discovered.note: Spartan society organizes around a helot-farmed economy and lifelong military training.

name: Greco-Persian Wars
fact: 300 Spartans held Thermopylae for three days against Xerxes's Achaemenid army.

discovered.note: Leonidas and 300 Spartans hold Thermopylae against Xerxes's invasion.

name: Peloponnesian War
fact: 27 years of Athens against Sparta, ending with the Athenian fleet trapped ashore.

discovered.note: Athens surrenders to Sparta, ending the 27-year Peloponnesian War.

name: Thales of Miletus
fact: Greek philosopher, c.624–546 BCE, credited as the first in the West to seek a rational rather than religious answer to what the cosmos is made of.

name: Pythagoras
fact: Greek thinker, c.570–495 BCE, who taught that number and mathematical ratio underlie the structure of the whole cosmos.

name: Heraclitus
fact: Greek philosopher, c.535–475 BCE, who held that the cosmos is in constant flux, held together only by tension between opposites.

name: Parmenides
fact: Greek philosopher, c.515–445 BCE, who argued through pure logic that reality is a single, unchanging, indivisible whole.

name: Protagoras
fact: Greek Sophist, c.490–420 BCE, who taught that truth is relative to the individual: 'man is the measure of all things.'

name: Democritus
fact: Greek philosopher, c.460–371 BCE, who with Leucippus held that only atoms and the void between them truly exist.

name: Mozi
fact: Chinese philosopher, c.470–391 BCE, who founded Mohism, teaching impartial, universal love (jian ai) for all people equally.

name: Diogenes of Sinope
fact: Greek founder of Cynicism, c.404–323 BCE, who lived by choice in a large storage jar and owned almost nothing.

name: Zeno of Citium
fact: Phoenician-Greek philosopher, c.332–265 BCE, who founded Stoicism in Athens after a shipwreck cost him his cargo.

name: Stoicism
fact: School founded by Zeno of Citium holding that the goal of life is to live in agreement with nature, mastering only what reason controls.

name: Socratic Method
fact: Socrates's technique of pressing a partner with question after question until their claimed knowledge collapses into contradiction.

name: Augustine of Hippo
fact: Christian philosopher, 354–430 CE, who argued evil is not a thing God made but a privation, an absence of good.

name: Boethius
fact: Roman philosopher, c.480–525 CE, who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution on a charge of treason.

name: St. Anselm
fact: Archbishop of Canterbury, 1033–1109, who devised the Ontological Argument: God, the greatest conceivable being, must exist in reality.

name: Averroes
fact: Andalusian judge and philosopher, 1126–1198, who argued philosophy and Islamic revelation cannot truly contradict, since both pursue truth.

name: Rumi
fact: Persian Sufi poet, 1207–1273, who taught that the soul rises through mineral, plant, animal, and human forms toward the divine.

name: Desiderius Erasmus
fact: Dutch humanist, 1466–1536, whose satire In Praise of Folly gives a mock speech in which Folly praises naivety over intellectual pride.

name: Niccolò Machiavelli
fact: Florentine political philosopher, 1469–1527, whose The Prince argues a ruler needs the ferocity of a lion and the cunning of a fox.

name: Michel de Montaigne
fact: French philosopher, 1533–1592, who retired to a tower to write his Essays, arguing the pursuit of fame corrodes true tranquility.

name: Francis Bacon
fact: English philosopher, 1561–1626, credited with 'knowledge is power' and the empirical, observation-based scientific method.

name: Thomas Hobbes
fact: English philosopher, 1588–1679, who argued man is purely physical, matter in motion, with no incorporeal soul — 'man is a machine.'

name: Blaise Pascal
fact: French mathematician and philosopher whose 1654 letters with Fermat founded probability theory.

name: Baruch Spinoza
