fact: Capital Suva. Taveuni's Rainbow Reef has earned Fiji's waters the name 'soft coral capital of the world.'

name: Samoa
fact: Jumped the International Date Line in Dec 2011, skipping 30 December to trade with Australia in real time.

name: Reflecting Telescope
fact: Newton's 1668 design swapped the lens for a curved mirror, killing the color-fringing that plagued refractors.

discovered.note: Isaac Newton builds the first working reflecting telescope.

name: Sextant
fact: Two mirrors double the measured angle, so a 60° arc can read up to 120° of sky.

discovered.note: John Hadley and Thomas Godfrey independently develop the double-reflection principle behind the sextant.

name: Adaptive Optics
fact: A laser fakes a star in the sky so a mirror can flex fast enough to cancel the atmosphere's twinkle.

name: Coronagraph
fact: An occulting disk in the telescope blots out a star's glare so instruments can see what's hiding beside it.

discovered.note: Bernard Lyot introduces the coronagraph.

name: Spectrograph
fact: Same prism as a spectroscope, but a camera behind it instead of an eye — the spectrum gets recorded.

name: Astronomical Interferometer
fact: Link two telescopes and their combined light resolves detail as fine as the gap between them.

name: Hubble Space Telescope
fact: A reflecting telescope orbiting above the blur of Earth's atmosphere, riding up on Discovery in 1990.

discovered.note: Space Shuttle Discovery launches the Hubble Space Telescope on mission STS-31, April 24.

name: James Webb Space Telescope
fact: 18 hexagonal beryllium mirrors, gold-plated to reflect the infrared light the telescope was built to see.

discovered.note: JWST launches on an Ariane 5 rocket, December 25.

name: Voyager Program
fact: Powered by decaying plutonium, not sunlight — why it still transmits from interstellar space 45+ years on.

discovered.note: Voyager 1 and 2 launch atop Titan IIIE-Centaur rockets.

name: Sputnik 1
fact: A 58cm metal sphere that did nothing but broadcast a radio beep — and started the Space Race doing it.

discovered.note: The USSR launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, October 4.

name: Apollo 11
fact: Two astronauts walked on the Moon while a third circled alone overhead in the command module.

discovered.note: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon, July 20; Armstrong and Aldrin walk the surface.

name: International Space Station
fact: Continuously crewed since November 2000 — the longest unbroken human presence off Earth.

discovered.note: The ISS begins continuous human occupation, November 2.

name: Curiosity Rover
fact: Its ChemCam fires a laser at rock from 7m away and reads the flash of vaporized plasma to tell what it is.

discovered.note: Curiosity lands in Gale Crater on Mars, August 6.

name: New Horizons
fact: A spare part built for the Cassini mission — its plutonium power generator — carried it past Pluto in 2015.

discovered.note: New Horizons flies by Pluto, July 14.

name: Cassini-Huygens
fact: Launched to Saturn in 1997, it dropped a probe onto Titan in 2005 — the only landing ever made past Mars.

discovered.note: Cassini-Huygens launches for Saturn, October 15.

name: Alpha Centauri
fact: Three stars, one system, and the nearest neighbors our Sun has — the closest just 4.2 light-years off.

name: Proxima Centauri
fact: The single closest star to the Sun — and it has a roughly Earth-mass planet sitting in its habitable zone.

discovered.note: Proxima b, an exoplanet orbiting Proxima Centauri, is confirmed, August 24.

name: Virgo Cluster
fact: Not close enough to hold onto us, but massive enough to slow our galaxy's drift away by about a tenth.

name: Halley's Comet
fact: Edmond Halley used Newton's laws to prove this comet keeps returning — and predicted the exact year it would.

discovered.note: Halley's Comet returns as predicted, confirmed by Johann Palitzsch, December 25.

name: Stellar Parallax
fact: Wait six months for Earth to cross its orbit, and a nearby star visibly shifts against the background sky.

discovered.note: Friedrich Bessel publishes the first reliable stellar parallax measurement, for 61 Cygni.

name: Settlement
fact: A permanent home base, no longer struck and carried onward after the harvest.

name: Cultural Hearth
fact: The place a cultural trait or practice is first invented, from which it then spreads outward.

name: Distance Decay
fact: Interaction between two places fades the farther apart they are — Tobler's First Law of Geography.

name: Culture Region
fact: An area unified by one shared cultural trait, strongest at its core and fading toward its edge.

name: Contagious Diffusion
fact: A practice spreading outward person to person, like a disease, with no regard for city size.

name: Hierarchical Diffusion
fact: An innovation leapfrogging straight to the biggest cities first, only later reaching small towns.

name: Stimulus Diffusion
fact: The core of a practice spreads, but gets reshaped to fit each new place it lands in.

name: Relocation Diffusion
fact: A practice carried to a new place in person, by someone who actually moved there.

name: Migration
fact: A permanent change of home, whether across town or across an ocean.

name: Push Factor
fact: A hardship at home — war, drought, no jobs — that drives people to migrate away.

name: Pull Factor
fact: An opportunity elsewhere — jobs, safety, freedom — that draws migrants toward it.

name: Urbanization
fact: The rising share of a population living in cities rather than the countryside.

name: Unitary State
fact: A country where the central government holds supreme power over every region.

name: Federalism
fact: Power split geographically between a central government and self-governing regions.

name: Separatist Movement
fact: An organized push by a minority group to fully break away from the larger country.

name: Self-Determination
fact: The principle that a people has the right to choose its own political status.

name: Census
fact: An official count of everyone living in a territory, ideally taken once a decade.

name: Electoral District
fact: A slice of territory whose voters elect their own representative to a legislature.

name: Gerrymandering
fact: Drawing electoral district lines to favor one party — named for an 1812 salamander-shaped map.

name: Primary Sector
fact: The part of an economy that extracts raw material straight from land or sea.

name: Secondary Sector
fact: The part of an economy that manufactures raw material into a finished product.

name: Tertiary Sector
fact: The service economy — retail, healthcare, transport — now most of US employment.

name: Quaternary Sector
fact: The knowledge economy split off from services around 1970: software, R&D, finance.

name: Factors of Production
fact: Land, labor and capital: the classic inputs every business must pay for.

name: Comparative Advantage
fact: The principle that a place should make what it produces most efficiently, and trade for the rest.

name: Footloose Industry
fact: A factory so cheap to relocate it can chase wherever labor is cheapest.

name: Gini Coefficient
fact: A single number from 0 to 1 measuring how unequally income is shared across a population.

name: Break of Bulk
fact: The point where cargo switches transport modes and must be unloaded and reloaded by hand.

name: Agglomeration
fact: The economic payoff of clustering close together — the basic reason cities exist at all.

name: Central Place Theory
fact: Christaller's model of how villages, towns and cities space themselves evenly across a plain.

name: Suburbanization
fact: The mid-20th-century population shift from city centers into car-dependent suburbs.

name: Redlining
fact: Government maps that outlined minority neighborhoods and marked them too risky for loans.

name: White Flight
fact: The mass departure of white residents as a neighborhood or city grows more diverse.

name: Gentrification
fact: Wealthier newcomers moving into a once-abandoned inner-city area, raising rents as they arrive.

name: Urban Sprawl
fact: Low-density development leapfrogging outward from a city with little planning.

name: Edge City
fact: A suburban node with more office space than downtown, that didn't exist before the 1960s.

name: Ghetto
fact: A district where one ethnic or religious group is confined, a term dating to 16th-century Venice.

name: Restriction Enzyme
fact: An enzyme that cuts DNA at one exact sequence — a bacterium's chemical scissors against invading viruses.

name: Cloning Vector
fact: A plasmid cut open at one site, ready to accept and carry a foreign piece of DNA.

name: Recombinant DNA
fact: DNA stitched together from two different sources into one molecule.

name: Bacterial Transformation
fact: A bacterium taking up foreign DNA from its surroundings and replicating it as its own.

name: Taq Polymerase
fact: A DNA polymerase from a hot-spring bacterium, stable enough to survive PCR's near-boiling step.

name: PCR
fact: Repeated heating and cooling that doubles a target DNA sequence millions of times over.

name: Gel Electrophoresis
fact: An electric field pulling DNA through a gel's mesh, sorting fragments from small to large.

name: DNA Hybridization
fact: Heat splits a DNA double strand apart; cooling lets matching sequences find each other again.

name: Southern Blot
fact: DNA sorted by gel, blotted onto a membrane, then probed to find one sequence in the mix.

name: Sahara
fact: The world's largest hot desert, roughly the size of the contiguous US, across North Africa.

name: Nile
fact: At 6,650 km, among Earth's longest rivers; its yearly flood built Ancient Egypt's farmland.

name: Amazon River
fact: Carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined, draining the Amazon rainforest.

name: Andes
fact: The world's longest continental mountain range -- 8,900 km along South America's Pacific edge.

name: Alps
fact: Europe's youngest, highest range, thrust up where the African and Eurasian plates collided.

name: Mediterranean Sea
fact: Nearly landlocked; it reaches the Atlantic only through the 14-km-wide Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Argentina
fact: Stretches from the Andes to the Atlantic; independence declared 1816 at the Congress of Tucuman.

name: Brazil
fact: Holds most of the Amazon basin and rainforest; the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas.

name: Chile
fact: A ribbon of land between the Andes and the Pacific -- over 4,300 km long, rarely 350 km wide.

name: Peru
fact: Once the heart of the Inca Empire, whose ruins at Machu Picchu still crown the Andes.

name: Colombia
fact: One of only two South American countries with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

name: Venezuela
fact: Home to the world's largest known oil reserves, which have shaped its economy for a century.

name: Bolivia
fact: The largest landlocked country in the Southern Hemisphere; a third of it lies in the Andes.

name: Ecuador
fact: Named for the equator itself, which its capital Quito sits almost exactly on.

name: Paraguay
fact: Landlocked and split into two regions by the Paraguay River, which flows past its capital.

name: Uruguay
fact: The only South American country lying entirely south of the Tropic of Capricorn.

name: Nigeria
fact: Africa's most populous country, from northern savanna to southern coastal rainforest.

name: Egypt
fact: Ancient civilization arose along the Nile's fertile floodplain, cutting through the Sahara.

name: South Africa
fact: Where the Atlantic meets the Indian Ocean; uniquely among nations it has three capitals.

name: Kenya
fact: Named for Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest peak, whose slopes the equator crosses.

name: Ethiopia
fact: One of only two African countries never colonized; fossils here rank among the oldest human ancestors.

name: Morocco
fact: Separated from Spain by just 14 km at the Strait of Gibraltar.

name: Algeria
fact: Africa's largest country by area; the Sahara covers most of its territory.

name: Ghana
fact: The first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, on 6 March 1957.

name: Tanzania
fact: Home to Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, and the Serengeti's migrating herds.

name: Senegal
fact: Its capital Dakar sits on the westernmost point of mainland Africa.

name: DR Congo
fact: Centered on the Congo, the world's deepest river, under Earth's second-largest rainforest.

name: Madagascar
fact: The world's fourth-largest island; over 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else.

name: France
fact: The 1789 Revolution overthrew the monarchy and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

name: Germany
fact: Unified into a single empire in 1871 under Prussian leadership, with Berlin as capital.

name: Italy
fact: Unified as a kingdom in 1861 on the peninsula that was once the heart of the Roman Republic.

name: Spain
fact: Spans most of the Iberian Peninsula, which it shares only with Portugal.

name: Portugal
fact: Borders barely changed since 1297, making it one of Europe's oldest stable nation-states.

name: United Kingdom
fact: Great Britain, part of Ireland, and thousands of smaller islands -- an archipelago nation.

name: Netherlands
fact: More than a quarter of the country lies below sea level, reclaimed from the sea since the 1300s.

name: Switzerland
fact: The Alps cover most of this landlocked country, neutral and war-free since 1815.

name: Poland
fact: Named for its flat terrain along the North European Plain -- from 'pole,' open field.

name: Russia
fact: The largest country on Earth by area, so vast it spans eleven time zones.

name: Greece
fact: Birthplace of Athenian democracy, scattered across thousands of Mediterranean islands.

name: Sweden
fact: Stretches roughly 1,600 km along the Scandinavian Peninsula, from 55N to 69N latitude.

name: Glycolysis
fact: Ten enzyme steps split one glucose into two pyruvate, right in the cytosol, no oxygen required. Net gain: two ATP, two NADH.

name: Pyruvate
fact: Glycolysis's three-carbon output, sitting at a metabolic fork: burn it for more ATP with oxygen, or ferment it to lactate without.

name: Krebs Cycle
fact: Pyruvate's carbons get stripped away one by one in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO2 and stacking up NADH and FADH2 to spend later.

name: Electron Transport Chain
fact: A relay of protein complexes in the mitochondrion's inner membrane passes electrons down an energy staircase to oxygen, pumping protons across as it goes.

name: ATP Synthase
fact: A molecular turbine: protons flowing back down the gradient the electron transport chain built spin its rotor, and each turn bolts a phosphate onto ADP.

name: Cellular Respiration
fact: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain running in sequence — about 30 to 32 ATP squeezed from one glucose molecule with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

name: Homeostasis
fact: Steady internal conditions held constant by active correction — blood sugar spikes, the pancreas releases insulin, and the level comes back down.

name: Diabetes
fact: Insulin production fails or cells stop responding to it, and glucose piles up in the blood instead of getting taken up for fuel.

name: Apoptosis
fact: Programmed cell death: mitochondria release cytochrome c, an apoptosome assembles, and a cascade of caspase enzymes dismantles the cell from the inside out.

name: Cell Cycle
fact: G1, S, G2, then M: growth, DNA replication, more growth, then division — checkpoints at each border refuse to let a damaged cell proceed.

name: Carbohydrate
fact: Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen roughly one-two-one. Starch and cellulose are both just glucose chained together — wired two different ways.

name: Nucleic Acid
fact: DNA and RNA — both built from repeating nucleotides, each one a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base.

name: Centrosome
fact: Two centrioles at right angles, wrapped in pericentriolar material — the cell's main microtubule organizing center, doubling before mitosis so each pole gets one.

name: Operon
fact: A cluster of genes run by one shared promoter, switched on or off together — E. coli's lac operon turns on only when there's lactose around to digest.

name: Transcription Factor
fact: A protein built to grab one specific DNA sequence, usually near a gene's start, and turn that gene's transcription up or down.

name: Oncogene
fact: A mutated or overactive version of a normal growth gene — push the cell cycle's accelerator hard enough and a tumor is what you get.

name: Nondisjunction
fact: Chromosomes fail to separate cleanly during meiosis, leaving one gamete with an extra copy and another one short — trisomy 21 is the most common survivable result.

name: Horizontal Gene Transfer
fact: Bacteria hand a plasmid straight to a neighbor through direct contact, no reproduction required — the main route antibiotic resistance spreads between species.

name: Endosymbiosis
fact: Mitochondria keep their own circular DNA and divide by binary fission — strong evidence they were once free-living bacteria engulfed over a billion years ago.

name: Tonicity
fact: Whether the outside of a cell is saltier (hypertonic), more dilute (hypotonic), or matched (isotonic) — tonicity decides which way osmosis pushes the water.

name: Turgor Pressure
fact: Water pushes the plant cell's membrane hard against its rigid wall from the inside — the pressure that keeps a plant upright without a single bone.

name: Pinocytosis
fact: Cell drinking: the membrane dimples around a droplet of fluid and pinches off as a vesicle, taking in whatever happens to be dissolved in it — no target required.

name: Quorum Sensing
fact: A bacterial population senses its own chemical signal building up; once it crosses a threshold, every cell switches behavior at once.

name: Genotype
fact: The specific alleles an organism actually carries — its genetic parts list, as opposed to what those parts end up building.

name: Phenotype
fact: What a genotype actually becomes once development and environment get involved — the traits you can see, measure, or catch a disease from.

name: Auxin
fact: A plant hormone made at the shoot tip. Darwin showed in 1881 that the tip senses light while the bend happens lower down; Frits Went isolated the chemical itself decades later.

name: Phototropism
fact: Auxin builds up on a stem's shaded side, making those cells stretch more than the sunlit side — the whole stem curves toward the light.

name: Ireland
fact: Britain ceded Dublin Castle, its seat of rule here for 700 years, to the new state in 1922.

name: Austria
fact: Full sovereignty was restored 15 May 1955, when Allied powers signed a treaty at Vienna's Belvedere Palace.

name: Türkiye
fact: In 2022 its government asked the world to use 'Türkiye' instead of 'Turkey', partly to avoid the bird's name.

name: Israel
fact: Independence was declared 14 May 1948; its Star of David was adopted by Zionists in Basel in 1897.

name: Lebanon
fact: Became a republic when French Mandate rule ended in 1943, choosing the ancient cedar as its emblem.

name: Saudi Arabia
fact: Ibn Saud's 1902 raid retaking Riyadh's Masmak fort began the conquest that unified the kingdom by 1932.

name: Iran
fact: Its Lion and Sun emblem, official since the Safavid era, was dropped after the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

name: Flag of the Netherlands
fact: Started orange-white-blue for William of Orange; orange faded to red, fixed by decree in 1937.

name: Flag of Ireland
fact: Green for Catholics, orange for Protestants, white between for peace; standardized in 1848.

name: Flag of Switzerland
fact: White couped cross on red, from the war flag of Schwyz; one of only two square national flags.

name: Flag of Austria
fact: Red-white-red, recorded on a 1230 abbey seal, is among the oldest state symbols still flown.

name: Flag of Greece
fact: Nine stripes spell 'Freedom or Death' in syllables; the cross recalls Greek Orthodox Christianity.

name: Flag of Türkiye
fact: The star and crescent flew on Ottoman flags by the 1840s; the Republic kept it unchanged in 1923.

name: Flag of Israel
fact: Blue stripes echo the tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl; the flag was adopted 28 October 1948.

name: Flag of Lebanon
fact: A cedar tree on red-white stripes, adopted 7 December 1943, days before independence.

name: Flag of Saudi Arabia
fact: Bears the Shahada above a sword, printed identically on both sides so the text always reads right.

name: Flag of Iran
fact: 'Allahu Akbar' repeats 22 times along its bands, marking the date of the 1979 revolution.

name: Flag of Japan
fact: The Hinomaru sun-disc is centuries old, but only became Japan's legal flag by statute in 1999.

name: Flag of South Korea
fact: Red-blue taegeuk for cosmic balance, with four trigrams; first flown under Joseon in 1883.

name: Flag of China
fact: Four small stars for the people's classes orbit one large star for the Communist Party.

name: Flag of Indonesia
fact: Nearly identical to Monaco's flag; Monaco's later objection to the resemblance was ignored.

name: Flag of Australia
fact: Its Commonwealth Star gained a seventh point in 1908, for the Territory of Papua.

name: Flag of New Zealand
fact: Four red Southern Cross stars on a Blue Ensign; voters chose to keep it in a 2016 referendum.

name: Flag of Papua New Guinea
fact: Designed by 15-year-old Susan Karike; adopted 1971, sharing the Southern Cross with Australia.

name: Metonic Cycle
fact: Almost exactly 19 years and 235 lunar months, after which the Moon's phases fall on the same calendar dates again.

name: Tumor Suppressor Gene
fact: The real stop signal: halts a damaged cell, or forces it to self-destruct. p53 is disabled in a third of cancers.

name: Tumor
fact: An uncoordinated mass of tissue growth. Most stay contained — invading nearby tissue is what makes one cancer.

name: Metastasis
fact: Cancer cells breaking off to colonize a distant organ — over 90% of cancer deaths trace to this.

name: Glioma
fact: Grows from the brain's glial support cells, not its neurons — about 80% of malignant brain tumors.

name: Melanoma
fact: Grows from melanocytes, the skin's pigment cells. Caused mainly by UV — the deadliest skin cancer.

name: Leukemia
fact: Begins in bone marrow and floods the bloodstream with abnormal cells, instead of forming one solid mass.
